minutes.headline: Conservation Commission approved the Lake Shirley boat ramp rebuild with wetland buffer waivers.
minutes.summary: The Lunenburg Conservation Commission held a long session covering multiple RDAs, NOIs, tree-removal determinations and a certificate of compliance, approving several routine wetland-adjacent projects (a cemetery expansion, septic repairs, a shed/sand permit, tree removals) with standard conditions. The major substantive action was approval of the Shady Point boat ramp reconstruction on Lake Shirley with buffer-zone waivers after public debate over impervious-surface classification and a retaining wall versus riprap; several other hearings (404 Page Street, 108 Sunny Hill Road, the Violet irrigation pond, 141 Pleasant Street) were continued to October 7. The commission also discussed Hollis Road residence budget items, a storm water utility warrant article, and a resolved no-trespass situation at the Pleasant Street Conservation Area.

what_happened.line: The commission approved the Lake Shirley boat ramp rebuild at Shady Point, granting waivers to work inside the normal 30-foot no-disturb and 50-foot no-build wetland buffers.
Four other wetland hearings, including a new house and driveway at 404 Page Street, were continued to October 7 rather than decided.
The commission approved three routine RDAs with standard conditions: a DPW cemetery expansion, a septic force main repair, and a shed/sand permit.
A non-binding warrant article was finalized asking whether storm water funding should move out of the operating budget into a dedicated storm water utility.
A vote on replacing flooring at the town-owned Hollis Road residence was deferred pending clarification of a vendor's deposit request.

why_it_matters: The boat ramp decision sets a precedent for allowing construction inside protected wetland buffers along Lake Shirley when a project shows a public benefit.

The storm water warrant article, if it reaches town meeting, would ask voters to decide whether storm water work gets its own dedicated funding stream instead of competing inside the general operating budget.
Residents near 404 Page Street, 108 Sunny Hill Road, the Violet irrigation pond, and 141 Pleasant Street will have another chance to be heard before any of those projects are decided.

budget_items.what_was_said: After reconciling impervious-surface data with the assessor's roll, the consultant said the final flat per-household number came out around this figure and the task force preferred a flat fee over calculating perable area per residence.
The task force said there were questions on four properties and that they had gotten answers, citing this figure in the discussion of one parcel.
Two properties approaching a million square feet were cited as an example of how high a utility fee could get for very large non-residential parcels.
A comparison town's abatement system was described as capping relief at this level, described as a powerful incentive for commercial property owners to improve stormwater management.

Agreed the task force needs to vote on the article language itself before it can be submitted, and that members cannot deliberate over email/BCC due to open meeting rules.

what_happened.line: The task force will ask a non-binding straw poll of town meeting to choose between a stormwater utility fee and continuing to fund stormwater work through the operating budget.
Members settled on billing every property a flat fee based on its impervious surface (an ERU approach) rather than tiered rates, if a utility is chosen.
Fees would be billed separately from the property tax bill, payable quarterly by tear-off coupon; municipal land would not be billed but churches and nonprofits would be.
A warrant article is due September 17, with two task force meetings around September 8 and 14 to draft and vote on its language before sending it to town counsel.
FinCom hears the proposal October 8, the Select Board October 20, and a public information session is planned around November 3, ahead of the November 17 special town meeting.

why_it_matters: Depending on which funding path town meeting favors in the non-binding vote, residents could see stormwater costs shift from the tax bill to a new separate utility bill tied to a property's paved and roofed area.
Churches, nonprofits and large commercial parcels would be billed under a utility approach even though they are often exempt from property tax, while town-owned land would not be billed.
The vote at town meeting is advisory only; the operating-budget alternative includes a stormwater engineer position that failed as an override once already.

meetings.summary: The Finance Committee held a public hearing on three warrant articles for a citizen-petitioned special town meeting, driven by new state aid the town received after the legislature's final budget exceeded the governor's January figure. The committee also approved prior minutes, heard committee reports, and decided to caucus informally at town meeting rather than hold a separate pre-town-meeting session.

minutes.summary: The Finance Committee held a public hearing on three warrant articles for a citizen-petitioned special town meeting, driven by new state aid the town received after the legislature's final budget exceeded the governor's January figure. The committee voted to recommend approval of article 1 (a school spending plan funded by that new state aid, including a second grade teacher, reading specialist, assistant principal, music teacher, literacy support, and reduced athletic transportation costs) and voted to defer articles 2 and 3 to town meeting itself, since article 2's petitioner plans to move to pass it over and article 3's funding source (a possible new special-purpose fund drawn from RAP money) had not yet been established by the Select Board or ratified by the School Committee. The committee also approved prior minutes, heard committee reports, and decided to caucus informally at town meeting rather than hold a separate pre-town-meeting session.

The committee deferred the second warrant article to town meeting itself, since its own petitioner plans to move to pass it over.

The committee also deferred the third article, covering middle and high school sports funding, because its funding source had not yet been established by the Select Board or ratified by the School Committee.

Town officials informally agreed to apply a school choice credit to reduce the amount needed for the sports-funding article, pending action by the Select Board and School Committee the following week.

why_it_matters: Residents will be asked to vote on all three warrant articles at the special town meeting, including whether to fund the school positions and restored athletic transportation described in article one.

The mechanism behind article three -- a possible new special-purpose fund drawn from RAP money -- was still undecided at this meeting, so what residents vote on for sports funding may change before town meeting.

Town counsel advised that the article three motion will be worded more generally than the printed warrant article, since town meeting cannot legally earmark school-budget funds for a specific purpose.

meetings.headline: Select Board unanimously ruled the dog is not a nuisance after a hearing where no witness reported evidence of nuisance behavior.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board held a public hearing under MGL c.140 §157 on a nuisance-dog complaint filed by George and Jennifer Burden against neighbors Charles and Stacy Cordmash. The complainant declined to testify, while the investigating detective, the animal control officer, the dog owner, and a neighboring HOA trustee all testified that they found no evidence of excessive barking or other nuisance behavior; after deliberation the board voted unanimously that the dog is not a nuisance dog, and town counsel was asked to draft the written decision and to consider changing the hearing process going forward.

minutes.summary: A joint Select Board / Lunenburg Municipal Building Design Committee meeting opened with a presentation on Mass Save energy-summit incentives for building electrification, then shifted to a long workshop on the deteriorating TC Pacios (TCP) building — its failing systems, a history of a double-appropriated roof-repair fund later corrected at town meeting, and whether to repair or demolish it. what_happened.line: Select Board and the building design committee leaned toward demolishing TC Pacios rather than repairing it, with no formal vote taken.
The Facilities Director was tasked with cost estimates for either a roof replacement or asbestos abatement plus full demolition, to feed the FY28 capital plan.
A roof-repair fund had been double-appropriated after a 2023 transfer was never reflected in MUNIS; town meeting corrected it this past May.
Election voting equipment and polling are being permanently moved out of TC Pacios to the schools, with a mobile trailer for storage.

why_it_matters: Whether TC Pacios is repaired or demolished will shape the FY28 capital plan and what residents are asked to fund next.
The building's boiler failed a required state inspection and needs repair within 30 days or the town faces state fines, a cost pressure independent of the long-term decision.
Moving the polling location and election storage out of TC Pacios changes where some residents vote.

meetings.headline: The Select Board called a citizen-petition special town meeting for September 3, setting the warrant and hearing schedule.
meetings.summary: The Select Board set the schedule for a citizen-petition special town meeting for September 3, 2026, working through a tight statutory timeline for the warrant, legal ad, FinCom public hearing and mailed notices, complicated by town moderator Tim Murphy's unavailability that date. The board also approved the September 1 state primary election warrant and ratified the DPW collective bargaining agreement with Teamsters Local 170, then adjourned to meet again the next evening in a joint workshop with the Municipal Building Design Committee.

The board decided to stick with the Ledger for consistency with what residents expect to read.

Approve the September 1, 2026 state primary election warrant.
Ratify the collective bargaining agreement with Teamsters Union Local 170 (DPW).

The board also reviewed a draft library space-use agreement it declined to sign, discussed reciprocal field usage with the school district, and voted to appoint a commissioner to the town's Open Space Committee and to approve two sets of minutes.

budget_items.topic: Town Beach fee increase vs. actual revenue
budget_items.what_was_said: The recreation director said the May rate increase brought in more money but not as much as hoped when the in-town rate was raised; the department had expected a larger increase than it is seeing.
The town-appropriated salary line for Town Beach was already mostly spent two and a half weeks into the season; going over it means drawing from the beach revolving account.

budget_items.topic: Day-pass revenue, same date year over year
budget_items.what_was_said: Day-pass money collected by the same date this year was compared to last year to help judge whether an extra open week would be worth the cost.
Total dollar value of beach passes sold so far this year was compared to the full prior year, with the current season not yet finished.
Swim lesson revenue rose year over year even though an afternoon session was dropped, with fewer staff running the program.

budget_items.topic: Cost to staff an extended beach week
budget_items.what_was_said: A bare-minimum two-lifeguard shift for an extra week was estimated in daily salary cost and weighed against whether day-pass sales would cover it.
An unlocked irrigation controller was changed by a user group to run far longer than intended, producing an unusually high water bill; a lockable controller has since been installed.

budget_items.topic: Water district billing detail, Marshall Park
budget_items.what_was_said: Three separate water district charges on the same billing date were reviewed, one much larger than the other two, plus a further large charge the following quarter.
A commissioner noted the school district's community-schools program charges a fee to play in its adult men's basketball league, seen as competing revenue with Parks programming.
The department's outsourced field-mowing contract was described as recently renewed for a multi-year term, itemized by field, with overage billing when extra mowings are required.

decisions.decision: Hold off deciding whether to extend the Town Beach season until more revenue and weather data come in and the town accountant can weigh in.
Not to sign the draft library space-use agreement yet; wait to hear the library trustees' specific concerns first.
Lock all park irrigation controllers and check them periodically following the Marshall Park billing incident.
Ask facilities to identify which field each water bill on the budget report corresponds to.
Target the Town Beach renaming ceremony for around September 10th, pending the sign's completion and family availability.
Move the next scheduled September meeting from the 23rd to the 30th due to member absences.

what_happened.line: The board set a path toward deciding whether to demolish or renovate the deteriorating TCP building, asking the Municipal Building Design Committee for a formal recommendation to feed fall capital planning.
The board directed staff to draft its overdue, town-meeting-directed report on selling or long-term leasing the Brooks House, targeted for completion by the fall town meeting.

why_it_matters: Whichever way the TCP decision goes, the cost was described as able to consume most or all of a year's capital plan, which shapes what other town projects can be funded that year.
The Brooks House report determines the town's public path for a building it has been directed by town meeting to resolve, and residents may see options at a future town meeting.
Financial policies under discussion -- OPEB funding, reserves, and revenue projections -- bear on the town's long-term borrowing capacity and, eventually, the tax rate.

meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board ratified a police detective promotion and several routine appointments, heard a lengthy planning-director update and a historical society pitch for a Revolutionary War memorial, and got tangled in a dispute over a stalled Trust Fund Commission appointment. It also acted on several money and process items — adopting the IRS mileage rate, taking an eminent-domain easement for the Flatill Road bridge, designating the Cable Advisory Committee as special municipal employees, choosing police over a constable for three upcoming elections, and approving minutes including newly released executive-session employment agreements — while tabling the DPW union contract, the special election warrant, and the trust fund appointment, and deferring a decision on a special town meeting for additional state education funding.

The town manager reported progress on a temporary food pantry site at the former School Street school, the awarded Flat Hill Road Bridge contract, and a dangerous/nuisance dog complaint headed to a standalone hearing; the board also scheduled a July 14 goals workshop, approved several sets of prior minutes, heard numerous committee reports, and voted to enter executive session on non-union personnel matters.

meetings.headline: Committee debated reopening FY27 school budget after new state Senate aid, but leaned toward not disturbing the town-meeting-approved budget
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee spent most of the meeting debating whether newly-added state Senate aid should prompt reconsideration of the FY27 budget just approved at town meeting, with members split between honoring the town-meeting result and revisiting free cash, reserve, and OPEB policies given the tight fiscal situation. No formal budget action was taken; the only votes were procedural approval of past minutes and adjournment, while the committee set its next meeting for June 11th and agreed to revisit financial policy work and the tri-board process ahead of FY28.

A member noted that a sum the senator secured for Lunenburg last year likely ended up as part of the free cash built up through conservative budgeting.
The chair said current policy sets a $50k minimum reserve but allows up to roughly a 0.5% cap, giving flexibility for tight-budget years.

A resident asked whether a large sum moving through the state Senate has been specifically directed to Lunenburg; the chair said it is still working through reconciliation and has not been signed into law.
A resident described the cost of replacing PFAS-contaminated firefighter turnout gear as a large, currently unaddressed capital-type need, having discussed it with the fire chief months earlier.

Local receipts have not come in below a certain level for the past decade; this year's estimate was set lower and then adjusted upward slightly by the town manager. A member argued for reconsidering how conservatively local receipts are projected given the current budget strain.
A member asked how much free cash the town has this year and historically; the chair gave a rough figure and acknowledged not having the full ten-year history on hand.
The town currently puts a set percentage into OPEB annually per policy; a member questioned whether that approach should be revisited given current budget pressure.
A resident said he was told banks and bonding companies expect continued OPEB-type contributions, citing a large unaddressed liability, and argued token contributions would not be adequate.
The school committee is expected to bring forward a plan for Turkey Hill that will involve a major rebuild or rehabilitation; the town is currently well positioned financially to handle it.

A resident raised concern about reported structural issues with the school bleachers area, which a member confirmed has been discussed at the capital planning committee as an item exceeding normal capital thresholds.

meetings.headline: Override failed; committee accepts a balanced-budget of cuts and eyes another override attempt next year
meetings.summary: The committee processed the fallout of the failed override, with the superintendent outlining the resulting cuts (class sizes, interventionists, middle school sports and transportation, high school world language) and recommending the district implement the balanced budget and form a community task force rather than return to voters immediately. The committee elected new officers for 2026-2027 -- Laura as chair, Tony as vice chair, Mandy Gilman provisionally as secretary -- adopted several revised policies (cash handling, student data privacy, medication administration, advertising), tabled the fifth-grade bus-release procedure pending community feedback, and voted a composite evaluation of the superintendent's first year.

meetings.summary: The Select Board acknowledged the resignations of the vice chair (citing health, amid the aftermath of the failed override) and two town staff members, then reorganized its own leadership, electing a new chair, vice chair and clerk. It also voted on an ambulance-billing write-off, a nuisance dog investigation, waivers for a town event and a right of first refusal, discussed possibly calling a special town meeting on the budget while deferring to the School and Finance Committees, and heard a town manager's report on bridge and flooring project bids and a culvert grant.

meetings.headline: Select Board held final public comment on the override before Saturday's town election; the chair backed a yes vote.
meetings.summary: The Select Board held its final public comment session before Saturday's annual town election and Proposition 2½ override vote, hearing residents both for and against the override, then the chair publicly stated support for the override. The board also ratified a police executive assistant hire, approved two youth achievement proclamations, assigned a police officer (not the elected constable) to cover the election, approved an FY27 state advocacy letter on school funding, voted to sell two tax-title Hollis Road parcels, and entered executive session at the close.

budget_items.what_was_said: A resident argued the town's roughly $1.4 million in new growth revenue was split unevenly, with capital projects, a finance committee reserve above policy, and a new town manager hire funded while schools were left short of level-service funding.
A resident said the added annual tax bill under the override was unreasonable given current gas prices, citing figures for homes in a stated value range.
The board was asked to approve appointing Kimberly Murphy at a specific wage step in addition to ratifying her hire.
The board's advocacy letter urges the senator to increase circuit breaker funding to a stated reimbursement percentage under a specific line item.

Board agreed to aim to complete the town manager's annual evaluation the week following the town election, once outstanding board member input is compiled.

what_happened.line: The Select Board held its last public comment session before Saturday's override election, and the chair stated personal support for a yes vote.
The board agreed to assign a police officer rather than the elected constable to cover election day, after members raised concerns about the constable's public remarks on the override.

The advocacy letter and property sale don't change any resident's tax bill directly, but the letter is the town's on-record ask for state school funding changes that could affect future budgets.

minutes.headline: Town meeting passed the FY27 budget and sent two Prop 2½ overrides to a townwide ballot vote.
minutes.summary: Lunenburg's annual town meeting passed a full slate of warrant articles, most consequentially the FY2027 balanced town/school budget and a two-tier Proposition 2½ override package that, if approved by voters at the ballot in two weeks, would restore cut positions and programs in town departments and schools. Extensive public debate covered the balance budget's cuts to school staffing, the library, recreation, and public safety, a new assistant town manager position, and an alternative permanent-investment-trust proposal, before the body voted to approve article 10 and both override tiers under article 11, along with capital, PEG, salary-schedule and union-contract articles.

what_happened.line: Town meeting approved the FY27 town and school budget, then sent two Proposition 2½ override tiers to a townwide ballot.
The override votes followed debate over cuts to school staffing, the library, recreation and public safety in the underlying balance budget.
A proposal to fund town operations through a permanent investment trust instead of recurring overrides was raised but not adopted.
Town meeting also approved capital funding, PEG cable funding, the non-union salary schedule, and first-year contracts for the fire, municipal employees' and DPW unions.
The final article, covering TCP building decommissioning costs and a special assistant position in the assessor's office, was still under discussion when the recording ended with no vote captured.

why_it_matters: The two override tiers now go to a townwide ballot; that vote decides whether cut school and town positions and programs are restored and affects the property tax bill.
The FY27 budget that passed is a balance budget built around the cuts described at the meeting, so its effects take hold unless the ballot overrides pass.
The union contracts and salary schedule approved at the meeting affect town and school staff pay regardless of how the override vote turns out.

minutes.headline: Town meeting passed the FY27 town budget and sent both Prop 2½ override questions to a townwide ballot.
minutes.summary: Lunenburg's annual town meeting adopted a level-services FY27 town/school budget requiring deep staff and program cuts, then separately approved (for the ballot) a tier-one $2.4 million and tier-two $3.3 million Proposition 2½ override, each restoring cut positions in town departments and schools if voters approve. The meeting also acted on dozens of other warrant articles covering capital funding, union contracts, free-cash transfers to reserve funds, the closure and decommissioning of the TC Pacios building (displacing the food pantry, PEG studio and gym), a new assistant town manager position, a revised town-meeting notice policy, and transfer of Kids Kingdom playground land to the select board.

what_happened.line: Town meeting adopted a level-services FY27 town and school budget that requires cuts to staff and programs.
Town meeting separately approved two Proposition 2½ override questions, sending both to a townwide ballot; either would restore some of the cut positions if voters approve.
Town meeting approved closing and decommissioning the TC Pacios building, after ruling a floor amendment to fund food-pantry relocation costs outside that article's scope.
A new assistant town manager position was created and the current post retitled HR director, and future town-meeting notices move to a postcard/opt-in system.
Care and custody of part of the Kids Kingdom playground land was transferred from the school committee to the select board.

why_it_matters: Residents will be asked to vote yes or no on the two override questions at the ballot; the outcome decides whether staffing and programs cut from the base budget are restored.
TC Pacios housed the food pantry, the PEG public-access studio and a gym, and the building's closure means those users need a new location before it is decommissioned.
The new administrative position and the switch to a postcard/opt-in mailing change both the cost of town administration and how residents learn about future town meetings.
watch_next: The townwide ballot vote on the tier one and tier two Prop 2½ overrides
Relocation of the food pantry, PEG studio and gym before TC Pacios closes, expected around this year's heating season

meetings.headline: Schools urged town unity ahead of the override vote; routine grants and policy readings were approved
meetings.summary: The meeting was dominated by the superintendent and chair urging the town to approach the upcoming Proposition 2½ override and town meeting collaboratively rather than divisively, describing this year's tri-board budget process as unusually transparent. The committee also heard a LEAF Foundation fundraising update, approved two state grant submissions and a farm-to-school grant, discussed a scholarship trust/EIN dispute with the town's Trust Commission, revisited unified sports options, reviewed the quarterly budget and personnel reports, assigned negotiating teams for two union contracts, set a process for the superintendent's evaluation, and waived first readings on four policies.

meetings.headline: Public comment turned into a pitched fight over the FY27 override, staffing cuts, and a disputed Ledger story.
meetings.summary: The bulk of this meeting was public comment: the fire chief, both police and fire union presidents, a school committee member speaking as a parent, and residents disputed a local newspaper's coverage of the FY27 balanced budget, override, and staffing cuts, followed by lengthy rebuttals from board members and the Town Manager. The board also handled routine license and event-permit hearings, a town manager's report, tax-title property and cover-photo votes, committee reports, and voted to enter executive session over opioid-litigation settlement strategy; no vote was taken on the override itself.

minutes.headline: Public comment turned into a pitched fight over the FY27 override, staffing cuts, and a disputed Ledger story.
minutes.summary: The bulk of this meeting was public comment: the fire chief, both police and fire union presidents, a school committee member speaking as a parent, and residents disputed a local newspaper's coverage of the FY27 balanced budget, override, and staffing cuts, followed by lengthy rebuttals from board members and the Town Manager. The board also handled routine license and event-permit hearings, a town manager's report, tax-title property and cover-photo votes, committee reports, and voted to enter executive session over opioid-litigation settlement strategy; no vote was taken on the override itself.

what_happened.line: Public comment and board rebuttals covered the FY27 override, staffing cuts, and disputed newspaper coverage, but no vote was taken on the override.
The fire chief and firefighters' union president defended a proposed fourth fire shift, saying the staffing plan has not changed since last July.
The police union president disputed characterizations of town free cash as an available surplus, calling it one-time money for capital needs.
The Town Manager publicly rebutted a newspaper's article point by point on free cash, the deficit, and other disputed claims.
The board tabled a decision on selling two tax-title Hollis Road parcels until members can visit the properties.

why_it_matters: The dispute over budget figures and staffing plans bears directly on how residents weigh the FY27 override at town meeting.
Fire and police staffing levels discussed here affect emergency response coverage funded by the override.
Whether the town sells or keeps the Hollis Road parcels affects future town land use and potential revenue.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to recommend the FY27 balanced budget for town meeting.
The board recommended the override's second tier by a 3-1 vote; the first tier's vote outcome was not audible on the recording.
Public commenters objected to proposed cuts to the library, senior center and beach program alongside new spending on an assistant town manager and a fourth fire shift.
The board also recommended the PAC/PEG, solid waste, water and sewer enterprise fund articles, all unanimously.
The board scheduled a budget public information meeting for the evening of April 28 at the Adult Activity Center.

why_it_matters: Both the balanced budget and the override now go to town meeting, where the choice is between a level-services budget with cuts to programs like the library, senior center and beach program, or an override that funds the assistant town manager position and a fourth fire shift.
A resident weighing the override should note the split board vote on its second tier, which signals the choice was not unanimous even among the officials recommending it.
The April 28 public information meeting is the town's forum for residents to ask about the budget and override before voting.

what_happened.line: Finance Committee voted 4-2 to recommend both tiers of a Proposition 2½ override for town meeting.
The FY27 omnibus balanced budget was recommended on a split 4-1-1 vote after a member argued it under-documents two new positions.
The committee voted 4-2 to add the assistant town manager and HR director positions to the salary grid, which a member said bypassed the town's normal job-description process.
Several prior 5-0 and other warrant-article recommendations were re-voted so the chair's vote could be added before the warrant is finalized.
The next Finance Committee meeting was set for April 23, skipping April 9.

why_it_matters: Town meeting will vote on both override tiers as well as the underlying FY27 budget, so a resident's tax bill depends on which of these articles pass.
Adding the two new town-hall positions to the salary grid affects what those roles cost the town, and the committee's recommendation was split, not unanimous.
The re-votes and the finance committee's own annual report will accompany the warrant residents receive by mail before they vote.

budget_items.what_was_said: A new revolving fund would let the economic development committee handle sponsorship money for events like the meet-and-greet without it passing through the town's general accounts. FY2027 spending cap discussed.

Spending limits were read for ambulance billing, timber rights, school custodial special details, Green Thumb, library, Council on Aging, storm water task force, electric/gas/plumbing inspector, technology, wetlands protection fees, COA meal site, and parks programming revolving funds.
Two outstanding invoices to Aeroseptic were named as the only known prior-year bills so far; recommendation deferred to town meeting since more may surface.

budget_items.topic: FY26 closeout / snow and ice deficit
budget_items.what_was_said: The current estimated operating deficit, driven mostly by snow and ice removal, was given; transfers will cover part of it and up to a stated amount was earmarked from free cash pending final snow and ice bills.
Two override tiers would go to voters as separate ballot questions, with only the highest approved amount implemented; the Finance Committee deferred taking a position pending the full board.

An accounting error had moved the same unspent FY23 capital funds through two prior votes (TCP roof repair, then FY26 capital); this article unwinds both so the money returns to the FY26 capital plan cleanly.

Individual capital items were read out including DPW bridge completion, a police cruiser, a fire engine/brush truck, primary school entry/driveway and playground design, public safety building roof and boiler work, door security intercoms at Turkey Hill and the primary school, and a DPW front-end loader.
The planned motion would transfer this amount from solid waste enterprise revenue to operate the program for FY2027; the fund does not cover recycling costs.
The fund would use enterprise revenue to pay Fitchburg for water and recoup a percentage under an intermunicipal agreement; figures were based on usage estimates.
A transfer toward the sewer enterprise's share of retiree health benefit liability; a member asked why the PEG/PAC enterprise carries no similar contribution.
Total FY2027 operating budget figure for the sewer enterprise fund.

budget_items.topic: SAP salary schedule / cost of living adjustment
budget_items.what_was_said: A cost-of-living increase for non-union salaried employees would be funded from the salary reserve; a member clarified it is not tied to any federal COLA figure.

budget_items.topic: Special appropriation: TC Pasio and assessor position
budget_items.what_was_said: Funds requested for TC Pasio operating and decommissioning costs and for a special assistant to the assessor position.

budget_items.topic: Free cash to OPEB trust fund
budget_items.what_was_said: Ten percent of certified free cash was described as being transferred to the OPEB trust under the town's financial policy.
A second consecutive year of a small deposit was proposed to build a cushion against retirement buyout costs exceeding the operating budget line.
Funds requested for activities marking the town's 300th anniversary; some members felt the amount was too large given past reliance on volunteers.
A standard annual transfer from free cash to the general-purpose stabilization fund, distinct from the vehicle/special purpose fund.

A new deposit was proposed as a cushion against a future spike in health insurance costs; total town and school insurance costs across active and retiree accounts were estimated. One member asked for defined trigger criteria for using the fund before supporting it.

budget_items.topic: Vacation accrual system transition liability buyout
budget_items.what_was_said: The town proposed buying out the full accrued-vacation liability at current dollar value ahead of a transition to a continuous accrual system, covering SAP employees and settled/near-settled union groups.
A member recalled roughly this figure as the cost of printing and mailing full warrant booklets to every household, cited in favor of switching to a postcard notice.

budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager approved three capital requests: two feasibility studies for the primary school (playground and drive/playground) and camera systems for building entrances. Other requested items were deferred for later in the year due to funding and the Pacios building situation.

The district is seeking one-time federal earmark funding to build a district-wide instructional framework and offset a projected cut to Title One funding; the district would not have to make up any shortfall if the full amount isn't awarded.
Funds previously voted to be accepted from the scholarship fund were not actually transferred from the estate to students due to a legal/executor issue; the district will bring it back once resolved.
As of month-end the district was at 66.1% of budget expended, rising to 68.6% once a payroll posted; last year the district was at 67% at the same point, having spent less overall.
The collaborative tuition line is overspent because circuit breaker reimbursement money has not yet been posted back into it; this is described as a normally hard line to budget.

Electrical spending is running over budget due to a colder winter and last year's underbudgeting; gas/heating has money remaining, and next year's electrical budget was adjusted based on recent actuals.
Legal expenses are running hot this year and the FY27 budget has been adjusted upward as a result.

The district described fee revenue collected over two periods and the fee schedule by family size and reduced-fee eligibility, and members debated the fairness of the fee against the roughly $70,000 it raises given the district's financial situation.

Chapter 70 does not include transportation costs at all, and regional districts get 75% of transportation reimbursed while Lunenburg does not, which a member said could be worth a large additional sum if reimbursed similarly.

The adult men's basketball program generated minimal revenue per player and relies on unpaid volunteer facilitators; the adult health and fitness program is a pass-through to a private vendor with the district retaining no financial benefit, supporting the recommendation to discontinue the district-run program.

A draft letter to legislators notes Lunenburg ranks near the bottom statewide for per-pupil spending while spending well above the state-required minimum, which members attribute to flaws in how Chapter 70 categorizes districts.
A building-controls efficiency study at the high school may be covered up to 100% by the program, addressing malfunctioning thermostats and actuators causing temperature problems.
The existing landscaping contract for the district's three athletic fields has expired and is going out to bid; costs under the prior contract were described as escalating over the years.
The PTO reported raising a significant amount at a recent dance fundraiser, plus a separate Great Wolf Lodge fundraiser.

meetings.headline: Board set the FY27 town meeting warrant and voted a two-tier override question onto the town election ballot
meetings.summary: The Select Board worked through the annual town meeting warrant article by article with town counsel, deferring several items (prior-year invoices, FY26 budget adjustments, the snow-and-ice closeout, and union contract funding) to town meeting itself, and declining -- after individual members stated concerns -- to include a Trust Fund Commission legal-fees article or a quorum bylaw article that counsel flagged as legally uncertain. The board voted to place a two-tier Proposition 2½ override question on the annual town election ballot, rounding the tiers to clean dollar figures and choosing a "Question 1/Question 2" ballot format, while one member stated ongoing concerns about the override's affordability. It also discussed but did not finalize where the override and other articles should sit in the warrant order and consent agenda.

Clarified the "rule of necessity" legal doctrine behind the trust fund quorum article and said the commission has filed a breach-of-fiduciary-duty notice against the town with a 30-day response request.

minutes.headline: Board set the FY27 town meeting warrant and voted a two-tier override question onto the town election ballot
minutes.summary: The Select Board worked through the annual town meeting warrant article by article with town counsel, deferring several items (prior-year invoices, FY26 budget adjustments, the snow-and-ice closeout, and union contract funding) to town meeting itself, and declining -- after individual members stated concerns -- to include a Trust Fund Commission legal-fees article or a quorum bylaw article that counsel flagged as legally uncertain. The board voted to place a two-tier Proposition 2½ override question on the annual town election ballot, rounding the tiers to clean dollar figures and choosing a "Question 1/Question 2" ballot format, while one member stated ongoing concerns about the override's affordability. It also discussed but did not finalize where the override and other articles should sit in the warrant order and consent agenda.

what_happened.line: Board voted 5-0 to place a two-tier Proposition 2½ override question on the annual town election ballot, pending town counsel's final edits.

The board deferred several FY27 warrant items, including prior-year invoices and union contract funding, to town meeting itself.
A Trust Fund Commission representative told the board the commission has filed a notice of breach of fiduciary duty against the town.

why_it_matters: The override question, if it proceeds as set, will ask voters at the annual town election to approve additional property tax collection above the state cap, split into two tiers residents can vote on separately.

Sending prior-year invoices, FY26 budget adjustments, and union contract funding to town meeting itself means those costs will be settled by the voters present rather than decided in advance by the board.
The declined Trust Fund Commission articles and the fiduciary-duty notice point to an unresolved dispute between that commission and the town that may surface again at town meeting.

meetings.summary: The Select Board, Finance Committee and School Committee met jointly to finalize the structure and dollar figures of a Proposition 2½ override for the May town meeting and ballot, after months of separate budget work. They voted to pursue a two-tier override rather than one number, agreed to pull a stormwater utility request out of the override for now, and the School Committee raised its lower-tier ask to 1.6 million; officials could not guarantee the higher tier would prevent another override request next year, and the boards turned to planning joint public messaging before adjourning.

meetings.headline: School Committee locked in its override request; without it, elementary classes grow and sports/band busing are cut.
meetings.summary: The School Committee heard extensive public comment on proposed cuts to athletic and band transportation, middle school sports, and primary school staffing ahead of the next night's tri-board override meeting. The superintendent presented a revised balanced budget with both new positions (English learner teacher, restored assistant principals, special education teacher) and cuts (athletic trainer hours, several sports, transportation, custodial and technology lines), and the committee voted to accept that fallback budget while reaffirming its lowest override request as the one it will bring to town meeting.

meetings.headline: Committee picked one override number (core "Scenario C") and, if it fails, will cut athletic transportation to save a teacher and a therapy aide
meetings.summary: The School Committee spent most of a long meeting building two FY27 budgets: an override ask (core "scenario C," roughly $1.5-1.6 million) that it voted to send to the Select Board as a single number, and a "balanced" no-override budget that cuts classroom teachers, an assistant principal, a custodian, an occupational therapy assistant, and other positions through attrition. After extended debate over cutting athletics versus classroom staff, the committee voted to accept the balanced budget minus the athletic transportation line, directing the superintendent's team to decide how to reallocate that cut to restore a teacher and an occupational therapy assistant. Members also voted to formalize the town's PEC health-insurance opt-out enhancement, approved a scholarship payout, an international trip, and childcare-program handbook changes.

what_happened.line: The committee voted to send the Select Board one override number, built from a "core" budget option, instead of asking for two tiers.

It also voted to accept a no-override "balanced" budget but cut athletic transportation instead of a teacher, and told staff to find a way to restore that teacher and an occupational therapy aide position.
Members added back a small music-teacher position to the override budget to preserve fifth-grade band.
The committee voted to move forward on a richer health-insurance opt-out incentive for employees who decline coverage.
A resident in public comment asked, without answer in the minutes, what happened to money left over from a prior override.

why_it_matters: Town meeting voters will be asked to approve a single override figure built from this "core" budget, so this is the number that reaches the ballot.

meetings.headline: Board included nearly all FY27 warrant articles; TC Passios' safety issues leave the food pantry's future unresolved.
meetings.summary: The Select Board worked through most of the draft FY2027 annual town meeting warrant, voting to include (and in some cases recommend) dozens of articles covering capital cleanup items, union contract funding, an OPEB trust appropriation, a vacation-buyout liability reduction, and several bylaw changes, while holding off on the override placeholder, trust fund commission articles, a stormwater bylaw, and the Central Mass Mosquito Control article pending more information. The board also heard an extended, unresolved presentation from the Lunenburg Community Food Pantry about the deteriorating TC Passios building, where the food pantry currently operates, and closed a public hearing on opting out of mail-in early voting before entering executive session to discuss a collective bargaining agreement.

meetings.headline: Select Board leaned toward a two-tier (core + restoration) joint town/school override, no vote taken
meetings.summary: The Select Board spent a line-by-line workshop walking through every department's FY27 budget changes since the February 19 preliminary budget, flagging cuts (police clerk, second SRO, fire per diem, recreation director, communications/IT, animal control, town clerk staffing) as candidates to restore if an override passes. By the end the board leaned toward a tiered override structure (a core/level-service budget plus a separate restoration ask, for both town and school) but took no formal vote on it, and set a deadline of Thursday for the town's restoration number and Wednesday for the school committee's numbers.

what_happened.line: The Select Board leaned toward a two-tier override structure -- a core budget plus a separate restoration ask -- for both town and school, without taking a formal vote.

Board members worked line by line through department cuts made since the February 19 preliminary budget, flagging items such as a police clerk position, a second school resource officer, fire department per diem coverage, the recreation director post, communications/IT staffing and animal control funding as candidates to restore if an override passes.

The town manager was asked to produce the town's restoration budget number by Thursday, and Thursday's planned Tri-Board meeting was flagged for cancellation or reconsideration so the school committee's core and restoration figures could come in by Wednesday instead.

The board also settled smaller line items along the way, including pursuing a town engineer position in the restoration budget regardless of storm water compliance funding and leaving the snow and ice budget unchanged rather than risk a later cut.

why_it_matters: This is the shape of the override question residents may eventually vote on -- a base town/school budget plus a separate restoration ask, rather than one combined number.
The restoration list touches police staffing, a school resource officer, fire coverage, recreation programming and animal control -- services that stay cut if no override passes.

budget_items.what_was_said: The general fund free cash was certified this week; Karen Brochu was thanked for putting together the free cash submission to the state.
Bill Bernard presented an overall DPW budget higher than previous years, covering mandatory work, a new part-time clerk, restored pavement management, and MS4 storm water compliance money.

Bernard's budget restores pavement management to $650,000 'where it should be,' while the town manager's preliminary budget shows only $279,000; a committee member said they will not support the restoration in the final budget.

budget_items.topic: Catch basin cleaning and sweeping performance
budget_items.what_was_said: In-house work over the last three years has completed about 30% of catch basin cleaning and 22% of street sweeping, well short of what is mandated.
Bernard estimated it would cost about $100,000 less per year to contract out catch basin cleaning and sweeping than to hire three additional staff.
Bernard modeled a 3% annual increase for DPW, clerical union, and himself across FY25-27 to estimate roughly $52,000 in added salary cost, pending ongoing CBA negotiations.
The snow and ice budget is being increased 2.5% per year to close the gap between budget and actual spending, currently around $800,000.
Vehicle repair costs sent out to contractors exceeded the budgeted line significantly last year, prompting a requested increase.
The recycling budget was reduced after a closer look at actual spending; last year's budget was much higher than what is actually being spent.
The trash program is described as roughly self-funding at about $500,000 per year.
DPW cited a small bridge grant for the Flaill road bridge, a storm water asset management grant from the Mass Clean Water Trust, and a pending Mass Community Cover grant for engineering on a culvert.
Bernard plans to apply for a Complete Streets grant and has a cost estimate of about a million dollars for sidewalk construction and repair between the high school and Marshall Park.
Chapter 90 funding for FY27 is expected at a higher level than the typical amount; continuing at the higher level over several years would add nearly $1.7 million versus normal funding.
The sewer enterprise fund budget is just under $2 million, with expenses and revenues nearly balanced showing an estimated small surplus.
The town pays Leominster and Fitchburg to treat sewage since Lunenburg has no treatment plant of its own; this is the largest driver of the sewer budget.
The engineering line was budgeted at $30,000 last year but actual cost was $80,000 after DEP required additional engineering work; the line is being increased again.
Money is set aside to replace aging pumps, controllers, and pipe as the sewer system approaches the end of its design life.

Without a rate increase, user charge revenue was estimated to leave a large deficit; with the proposed rate increase the budget shows only a small surplus, avoiding further draws on retained earnings.
The proposed sewer rate increase is about 16%, driven by Leominster and Fitchburg raising their own disposal charges.

The per-unit user rate would rise from its current level to a higher figure (about 16% increase), while the minimum charge rises only about 5%, intended to soften the impact on lower-usage households.

budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager's budget rose substantially to fund a new assistant town manager position for a full year; restructuring by eliminating the communications/IT director position reduced the net new cost from $120,000 to $60,000.
Audit costs are rising because the town's former auditing firm was absorbed into a larger firm (CBIZ) at greater cost, and a competing firm lacked capacity to take on the town.
Small reductions were made to the treasurer and collector office budgets based on actual spending, including contracted services covering the deputy tax collector and Unibank services.
The assessor's budget is nearly level; a temporary special assistant position is being moved out of the operating budget to one-time funding; abatement counts have declined from a 2023 spike.
FY26 and FY25 real estate exemption counts and total dollar amounts were compared; the senior means-tested exemption was not approved for FY2025.
The town clerk's overall budget is roughly level, but the elections line rises sharply because 2026 is an election year with a September primary and November general election.
The APDC physicals budget was increased due to under-budgeting, and a new economic development committee line funds an annual town official meet-and-greet event.
The town report/printing line rose sharply because it had not been properly budgeted, covering the annual report, town meeting booklet, and special town meeting warrant printing and mailing.
The reserve fund is level funded; the town manager raised the idea of increasing it given department budgets are being tightened, citing prior years' transfer amounts.
The salary reserve has not been adjusted for FY27 pending outcomes of ongoing DPW, clerical, and firefighter contract negotiations; an anticipated 3% COLA for non-union (SAP) employees is assumed.
Central purchasing, which now includes consolidated postage costs, is level funded.
The veterans budget is largely driven by Chapter 115 benefit payments currently serving seven residents; the town receives trailing state reimbursement the following fiscal year.
This line rose almost entirely due to the non-discretionary Worcester County retirement assessment.
The unclassified budget, covering liability, workers comp, health, life insurance, unemployment and Medicare, increased from the preliminary figure due to a correction in Medicare supplement counts.
Liability insurance covers property/casualty with a rate guarantee through FY27, plus a separate injured-on-duty policy for police and fire and a small risk-management training line.
Workers compensation was reduced based on conversations with the town's insurance representative, applying available credits.
Group health insurance, the largest piece of the unclassified budget, increased; a separate line funds employees who opt out of coverage.
Retiree health insurance covers town and school retirees at estimated Medicare Blue and Medex rates, plus a Medicare supplement paid twice yearly.

what_happened.line: Finance Committee recapped a tri-board session where all members agreed an override belongs on the ballot, but remained split on whether it should be one amount or two.

DPW's proposed FY27 budget came in higher than prior years, restoring pavement management funding the town manager's preliminary budget had cut, though one committee member said they will not support that restoration.
The town manager's office is being restructured: the communications and IT director position would be eliminated and a new assistant town manager position funded starting July 1.

The committee recommended moving a warrant article seeking money to legally investigate several neglected municipal trust funds from the annual town meeting to a special town meeting, so a firmer cost estimate can be developed first.
The FY27 budget public hearing was pushed back one week to March 26, with a tri-board meeting taking the committee's March 19 slot instead.

why_it_matters: An override, once the ballot format is settled, would raise property taxes for residents and the one-question-versus-two split changes how they vote on it.
The DPW budget still has to be finalized, and whether pavement management funding is restored affects road paving work and how storm water permit compliance gets funded.
The town manager's office restructuring changes which staff position handles human resources and IT/communications duties going forward.

meetings.headline: TriBoard split near evenly on one FY27 override vs. two tiers, but agreed unanimously to put one on the ballot.
meetings.summary: The Select Board, Finance Committee and School Committee met jointly to debate how to structure a Proposition 2½ override for next year's budget, weighing a single combined ask against tiered options. Every member present favored putting some override on the ballot, but the group was closely divided over one number versus two, and no final figure was set that night. Town Counsel joined by phone to explain ballot procedure and campaign-finance limits, and the boards deferred a joint public statement, aiming to settle on a number in the coming weeks.

meetings.headline: Finance Committee warns a large school 'restoration' override could fail, as one did in 2012.
meetings.summary: The committee heard FY27 budget presentations from the Council on Aging (level-funded), the Library (a modest increase plus a push for above-level programming funding), and Public Access Cable, which described a widening deficit from declining Comcast franchise fees and a forced studio relocation. The bulk of the meeting was a debate over the upcoming Proposition 2½ override: members worried that bundling the town's mostly level-service requests with the school committee's much larger 'restoration' budget into a single ask risks a failure like the town's 2012 override, which passed by roughly two-to-one against and led to a decade of cuts.

public_comment.topic: Criticized the library presentation as too general with no itemized spending, and argued PAC should pursue nonprofit status and grants rather than seek town funding, citing pending state legislation he says is unlikely to pass soon.

what_happened.line: Finance Committee members leaned toward asking voters for a trimmed, level-service Proposition 2½ override rather than bundling town requests with the school committee's larger 'restoration' budget.
The concern was explicit: a 2012 override bundled similarly and failed by roughly two-to-one, leading to a decade of cuts.
The override's shape now goes to a tri-board meeting of town and school officials on March 10.

Public Access Cable described a widening deficit from falling Comcast franchise fees and a forced studio move, and agreed to start tracking how its staff time splits between government and public-channel work.
The Council on Aging presented a level-funded budget and the Library a modest increase, with a member asking the library to itemize all funding sources next time.

why_it_matters: Whether the town bundles a school 'restoration' ask into one override question or asks for less, level-service money affects every taxpayer's ballot choice and, town officials warned, whether any of it passes at all.
Public Access Cable's declining franchise-fee revenue and relocation could affect coverage of town and school meetings if the town doesn't take up funding it.
The library's state certification and state aid depend on the town meeting a minimum appropriation threshold, which this budget cycle sets.

what_happened.line: The Parks Commission voted to raise 2026 Town Beach season and day pass rates, aiming to shrink the town's subsidy of the beach program.
The Commission also voted, 3-0, to raise 2026 swim lesson rates, with a per-family cap for both residents and non-residents.
Staff said the new rates are still projected to fall short of covering the beach's costs, with the Parks revolving account as a possible backstop for the gap.
The Commission adopted an amended park facilities signage policy that removes the Commission itself from sign-approval authority, shifting it to staff.
Field-use rules and a proposed vendor-fair partnership were held off until a recreation director is hired, a position still vacant.

why_it_matters: This sets what residents and non-residents pay for beach passes and swim lessons in 2026, and it comes up in the context of a possible town override vote on covering town costs.
The rate increase is presented as narrowing, not closing, the gap between beach revenue and beach costs, so the shortfall may still draw on other town funds.
Sign approval at town park facilities now rests with staff rather than the elected Commission, changing who signs off on that kind of decision going forward.

meetings.headline: School Committee says only a townwide override can restore positions cut last year, not a smaller fix.
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee heard the IT department's FY27 budget request and a detailed FY27 school budget presentation focused on restoring special education, literacy, and student-services positions cut the prior year. No formal budget votes were taken; the meeting was discussion and Q&A ahead of a March 11 tri-board meeting where override strategy will be decided, with the School Committee chair stating a townwide operating override is necessary to avoid what he called "catastrophic" cuts.

budget_items.what_was_said: The IT department requested an FY27 budget reflecting roughly a 9% increase over the prior year, driven by loss of one-time ARPA funding for MUNIS, corrected telephone budgeting, and rising contracted services costs.
MUNIS was partly paid through ARPA in FY26 and now must be budgeted at full cost.
Reducing on-site IT support from 4 to a possible 3 days a week in FY27 would offset costs.
Not renewing Clear Gov software produces a savings that partially offsets other IT cost increases.

budget_items.topic: Adult Activity Center IT capital request
budget_items.what_was_said: A capital request for access points and server upgrades at the senior/adult activity center did not make the initial cutline but may be funded via a community compact IT grant.
The town breaks down its Microsoft licensing by tier: standard, basic, exchange, and premium, covering both employees and boards/committees.
A committee member questioned the cost of the Code Red emergency notification subscription relative to how many residents actually subscribe.
A portion of OpenGov's cost is offset by technology fees paid by users of online permitting, funneled through the tech revolving fund.

The superintendent gave the FY26 baseline: salaries, expenses, and a total that included a one-time free cash allocation used to offset health insurance, unemployment insurance, salaries, and athletic transportation.
School choice revenue received by the district has fallen sharply over the years, shifting that burden to the local taxpayer.
Extended day, lunch, and sped tuition circuit breaker were called out as the largest revolving revenue generators; the school choice "other" line includes bus fees collected early.
A member argued athletic fees should be required to cover athletic transportation costs, noting that doing so would wipe out the athletic revolving account.
Title I funding is expected to change significantly for FY27 versus FY26, with the district unsure of the exact allocation.
Title II, the main professional development funding vehicle, is projected lower for FY27.
Title IV funding, for safe and supportive school environments, is anticipated to be very small for FY27.
The special education entitlement grant largely funds one very expensive out-of-district placement at the May Institute/May Center.
Circuit breaker reimbursement is generally around a set percentage of the prior year's out-of-district tuition, rarely fully funded.
This is the second and final year of a two-year Student Opportunity Act grant, previously used to fund a literacy coach and now redirected to early literacy materials and professional development.
The state delegation secured earmarks for one-time costs; the FY27 amount is unknown, with prior earmarks discussed for use toward unfunded capital projects.
Health insurance is budgeted at current staff plans plus a percentage increase, plus new restored positions budgeted at the highest family plan tier as a conservative assumption.

The business manager budgeted a percentage increase for busing pending confirmation from the bus contractor, citing a memo with the actual contracted rate; the district has had four consecutive multi-year contracts with only one bidder.
Extra buses beyond the contracted set carry a per-bus, per-day surcharge on top of the base rate.

budget_items.topic: Total estimated cost of restored positions/restructuring
budget_items.what_was_said: The superintendent totaled the cost of all proposed restored positions and central office restructuring, assuming highest-tier health insurance for all new hires.
The business manager stated the full FY27 salary and expense totals that make up the override-level budget ask.

budget_items.topic: Budget line savings found before submission
budget_items.what_was_said: The superintendent and business manager found additional savings by revisiting the posted budget, partly by converting a proposed full-time athletic director into a half-time position.
Restoring the bridge program requires a teacher and a paraprofessional; costs were given separately for salary and insurance.

Proposed changes include eliminating a grant-funded literacy coach, moving a math coach to an instructional-specialist/teacher salary line, and adding a 0.5 data reporting manager and a 1.0 assistant business manager position.
A committee member questioned the cost of maintaining a full-time athletic trainer alongside a part-time athletic director as an outlier compared to peer districts.
A proposal to contract out social-emotional services (e.g., via Seven Hills or Community Health Link) was debated against keeping in-house school social workers given crisis response needs.

budget_items.topic: Proposed alternative to override: raise levy limit to invest
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident proposed increasing the levy limit to generate investment interest income as an alternative/supplement to an operating override, citing an estimated override figure and per-thousand tax impact.

reconciliation.what: Our minutes against the minutes the town published. caption_error = the same fact the captions rendered badly, resolved by the official reading shown beside the as-heard one; discrepancy = a substantive difference, flagged and not resolved. Neither record is treated as the referee.
reconciliation.summary: The two records cover the same meeting and agree closely wherever a hard number appears in both (grant totals, the FY27 school budget top-line, the health-insurance rate, the March 11 Tri-Board date), but ours captures a long tail of dollar figures, side-decisions and presenters — IT capital/software line items, the override/levy figures, several staffing-cost breakdowns — that the official minutes never mention at all, and several figures where the captions clearly mis-heard a digit. The one thing a reader should know: several "decisions" in our minutes (the single school budget line, the Microsoft breakdown commitment, the EPIMS staffing data commitment) have no counterpart anywhere in the official minutes, and the $996,123 restored-positions total does not reconcile with the sum of the official's own itemized staffing requests.

what_happened.line: Select Board voted by roll call to submit a three-item FY27 state earmark list: boiler upgrades, fire radios, primary school playground design.
The board dropped a bundled intercom/radio security request and the Fitzgerald field project after learning state guidance caps towns at one to three earmark requests.
Board ranked public safety building boiler upgrades as the top priority, ahead of fire department radios and the playground design.
The town manager will add justifications to the earmark letter and send it to all three members of the legislative delegation, not just one representative.
A separate Flat Hill supplemental budget request is being pursued by the delegation outside this earmark list.

why_it_matters: An earmark is a request for state funding outside the town's own budget, so dropping the school intercom and middle-high radio security upgrades from this list means that project now has to compete for town capital dollars instead.
The ranked order signals which project the delegation will push hardest for as the state budget moves through the legislature this session.
This affects the public safety building, the fire department, and the primary school -- not this year's town tax bill, since these are requests to the state, not town appropriations.

meetings.headline: Town Manager unveiled a preliminary FY27 budget that does not balance without a property tax override
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee heard FY27 budget presentations from the fire, facilities and police departments, each citing staffing, contract and equipment cost drivers, including a fire department fourth-shift staffing proposal and a police restructuring from two school resource officers to one SRO plus a second detective. The Town Manager then presented a preliminary town-wide FY27 budget that she said does not balance and currently relies on a Proposition 2½ override, walking the committee through revenue sources and expenditure categories in detail; no votes were taken on the budget or the override. She also reported that FY25 books were closed out late, risking a hold on state aid, though the town secured a filing extension.
