votes.motion: Motion to adjourn

budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager said free cash is not yet fully certified but is looking relatively healthy, aided by a Lunenburg public schools turnback and higher investment income.
The prior capital plan was premised on a lower estimated free cash figure that will now be revisited once free cash is certified.

budget_items.topic: Fire Dept total FY27 budget request
budget_items.what_was_said: The chief presented the total fire/EMS budget request, noting a typo, and said it represents about a 22% increase driven mostly by the fourth shift proposal.
The chief said nearly all of the fire budget increase is the fourth shift except for a smaller remaining amount.
Radio maintenance is proposed to rise because portable radio costs have skyrocketed.
Vehicle maintenance is increasing; the chief cited an ambulance with major repair costs and ongoing truck issues.
A requested increase covers farming out vehicle repairs the highway garage can't perform.
The emergency management line, mostly supplies, is unchanged.
The department typically receives a state grant for fire safety and senior safety education.
A multi-year firefighter safety grant, believed ended, reappeared this year and is being spent down.
This federal-through-state grant has not materialized this year amid federal funding disruptions.
The department typically receives donated funds for equipment not covered by the town budget.
One-time mitigation funds are being used for added predium staffing in FY26 and paramedic training in FY27; the chief cautioned these are non-recurring.
The department currently budgets a set number of weekly predium hours, concentrated on Sundays.
Sunday shift predium coverage for three people was quantified in the Q&A on staffing.
A stipend line funds on-call officer coverage on Sundays; it would go away with full career staffing.
The utilities budget rises largely because the TCP building's utility costs are finally being captured in the budget.
The town is adjusting how solar credits are allocated across buildings after accumulating a large surplus that can't be directly applied elsewhere.
The facilities maintenance budget is presented as roughly level service with targeted increases for repairs and contracted maintenance.
A mandated 20-year sprinkler head inspection found failures at the fire department requiring replacement, below the capital threshold.
The town's betterment cost for sewer installation expires after FY28, freeing budget room afterward.
The parks budget rises mainly due to purchase-of-service costs for landscaping and repairs.
The current landscaping contract doesn't cover enough mowing cuts for baseball season and would need additional funding to meet the needed frequency.
The revolving fund collects rent from public access TV and the Shapiro school leasing classrooms, offsetting TCP building costs.

A prior-year capital appropriation for the TCP roof was found to be double-counted with FY26 capital funding for town hall windows/HVAC design; a cleanup warrant article will rescind the original vote.
The police budget is mostly personnel costs driven by the collective bargaining agreement, stipends, overtime and training.

budget_items.topic: Police body armor and software costs
budget_items.what_was_said: Increases fund contractually required 5-year body armor replacement for six officers and new building-access software.
Hospital charges for new-hire physicals, psychological exams and drug tests have risen sharply, shared between police and fire budgets.
Vehicle maintenance is level-funded based on recent years' actuals, aided by cycling in two new cruisers annually.
The lockup line dropped substantially after the town began sending most male prisoners to the Worcester County Sheriff instead of holding them locally.
A state grant funds a co-response mental health clinician shared with Lancaster, which had been lost and then restored.
The department was not awarded its usual highway traffic safety grant this year, which normally funds radar units.
Comfort dog handling fees are a separate cost per dog; an unused second comfort dog would add another handling fee if utilized.
The Town Manager said the preliminary FY27 budget as presented is not balanced and relies on an override of this size, which she expects to keep changing.
Property tax, state aid, local receipts and enterprise funds were broken out as shares of total FY27 revenue.
Enterprise fund revenue is still being finalized pending sewer and PACK enterprise indirect cost work.
The maximum allowable levy calculation starts from last year's levy limit plus the allowable Proposition 2½ increase.

budget_items.topic: New growth, excluded debt, and maximum allowable levy
budget_items.what_was_said: New growth and excluded debt were added to reach the maximum allowable levy for FY27.
Actual new growth was compared to the estimate, with recent spikes attributed to catch-up assessments and a large commercial complex.

budget_items.topic: Total state aid and cherry sheet assessments
budget_items.what_was_said: Total state aid receipts, based on the Governor's budget, are offset by cherry sheet assessments.

budget_items.topic: Education aid and net school spending
budget_items.what_was_said: A portion of education aid does not automatically sweep to the schools because of net school spending rules.
The Town Manager raised, as a controversial option, potentially exiting the regional mosquito control program given its cost; exiting would require a town meeting vote.
School choice receiving tuition revenue has fallen sharply since before COVID, which a member said shifts cost onto Lunenburg taxpayers.
Investment income was budgeted conservatively but actuals came in far higher, prompting discussion of whether to budget more aggressively.
Investment income actuals have varied significantly year to year, described as market-driven and volatile.

budget_items.topic: FY25 local receipts, budget vs. actual
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted local receipts came in well above what was originally appropriated for FY25, arguing for less conservative budgeting.

budget_items.topic: FY27 starting revenue available for appropriation
budget_items.what_was_said: Total starting revenue for FY27, combining the levy, excluded debt and new growth, was presented before subtracting sweeps and assessments.
The assessors voted an overlay amount that is subtracted from available revenue.

budget_items.topic: Capital plan taxation and net revenue available
budget_items.what_was_said: An amount for the capital plan (level with last year) is subtracted, leaving the net revenue available for FY27 appropriations.

budget_items.topic: FY27 total expenditure increase, all categories
budget_items.what_was_said: Across all budget categories, the FY27 preliminary total increase over FY26 was presented as a specific dollar amount and percentage.
Maturing debt shows a small decrease from last year.
A member asked about the amount borrowed for turf fields, part of maturing debt.
This category, covering insurance and benefits, increases driven mainly by health insurance costs.
Workers comp was reduced based on several years of actual trends, described as not a service cut.
Active employee/retiree insurance is projected to rise based on the current plan, pending PEC negotiations that could change the figure.
Retiree Medicare supplement plan increases were estimated ahead of confirmed rates in the fall.
Despite higher underlying plan increases, the total health insurance line increase was smaller because the budget was rebuilt from actuals.
This category covering select board, town manager, accountant, assessors, treasurer/collector, IT, clerk and purchasing rises notably.
The increase partly reflects consolidating a PR/crisis communications contract fully into the select board office.
The town manager budget funds half a year of a new assistant town manager position, planned to start January 2027.
The town manager line's total increase is mostly attributable to the half-year assistant town manager funding.
An increase covers the annual audit cost, which was improperly budgeted in FY26, offset partly by retirement-driven wage savings.
Funding continues a temporary special assistant position created to complete DOR-mandated pre-revaluation work.
A small above-level increase funds additional training and a collector certification stipend.
A cost previously covered by ARPA funding must now be fully absorbed, offset by cutting the IT contractor to four days a week.
The town eliminated ClearGov software as a cost-saving measure.
An election-year increase drives up the town clerk, elections and registration lines.
The town report line rises because mailing costs for the annual and special town meeting books were previously underfunded.
Postage centralized from all departments into one line is being managed well at a level-funded amount.
Public safety overall rises substantially, driven by the fire fourth shift and police contractual obligations.
The police increase funds the contract while restructuring one sergeant, one SRO and adding one detective.
The fire increase funds the fourth shift and wage adjustments tied to an anticipated retirement vacancy.

budget_items.topic: Sealer of weights and measures contract
budget_items.what_was_said: A large percentage increase reflects a previously unbudgeted fixed-rate state contract discovered after the town stopped having a local sealer.
DPW's overall increase is driven by drainage, catch basin cleaning/street sweeping, and a new part-time administrative position.
An above-level request funds part-time help for the DPW executive assistant, who handles heavy invoice and grant reporting loads.
Continued above-level funding addresses a backlog of drainage work.

budget_items.topic: Catch basin cleaning and street sweeping (MS4 compliance)
budget_items.what_was_said: A large increase addresses required catch basin cleaning and street sweeping under the stormwater permit, though possibly insufficient for full MS4 compliance.
This line was reduced closer to actual line-striping costs.
The recycling line was reduced significantly after a deeper review of actual costs, with no program changes yet; a sticker/opt-in system is being explored with the hauler.
The overall facilities and buildings increase reflects contract negotiations and purchase-of-service needs.
Part of the increase is above-level funding for unanticipated high-cost repairs that don't meet the capital threshold.
The increase largely reflects fully budgeting the TCP building's operations.
This small budget category sees only a minor overall increase.
Regional health and nursing assessment increases were called displeasing given reduced service levels during a staff vacancy.
A shown decrease reflects uncertainty over final staffing configuration at the senior center and is likely to be revised upward.

budget_items.topic: Schools total budget (LPS and Monty Tech)
budget_items.what_was_said: Combined school budgets show a large increase; there was uncertainty whether the percentage is measured against last year's base budget or base-plus-supplemental funding.
LPS represents the bulk of the schools increase.
Monty Tech's increase was presented separately, previously discussed at an earlier meeting.
This small category increases mainly due to library programs and materials, offset by some decreases.
An above-level increase to library programs is offset by decreases to book services, alongside a materials increase.
This category is driven almost entirely by the Worcester Regional Retirement System assessment, over which the town has no discretion.
Tax title is unchanged from last year.

budget_items.topic: FY27 total budget vs. available revenue (deficit/override)
budget_items.what_was_said: The total presented FY27 budget exceeds total revenue available for appropriation, producing the deficit requiring an override.

budget_items.topic: New revenue available, FY27 over FY26
budget_items.what_was_said: New revenue growth was calculated and a portion allocated first to Monty Tech's increase before proportional distribution.

budget_items.topic: Proportional deficit split between schools and town
budget_items.what_was_said: If new revenue were distributed proportionally by each entity's share of the budget, the resulting deficits for schools and town were calculated separately, summing to the total override figure.
The town's PR contract covers crisis communications and regular monthly media stories, including national coverage of Officer McNamara's fraud case.
The Worcester County retirement assessment increase was clarified as roughly a 10% rise; it is a fixed bill the town does not control.
Nearly all of the intergovernmental line is Worcester County retirement, with a small remainder for MRPC.

transfers.description: A reserve fund transfer was needed last year to cover fire department vehicle maintenance overruns.

Prior-year capital appropriation intended for the TCP building roof will instead be redirected via a cleanup warrant article, after it was found to have been double-counted with FY26 capital plan funding for town hall window/HVAC design.

decisions.decision: Fire department will use Noba mitigation one-time funds for added predium (call staff) staffing in FY26 and set aside funds for paramedic training in FY27, rather than offsetting the fourth shift's ongoing cost.

The town will fund TC Pacios building operations through FY27 while winding down user groups, with the goal of not heating it through another winter and a possible decommissioning warrant article next year.
Police department plans to reconfigure staffing from two School Resource Officers to one SRO plus a second detective, focused on rising cyber/internet crimes against children.

The town will phase in a new full-time Assistant Town Manager position starting January 2027, funded for half the fiscal year, while the current Assistant Town Manager/HR position becomes HR Director with no salary change.
A public presentation on the fire department's fourth shift proposal is scheduled for the following Monday at the Adult Activity Center.
A Finance Committee public hearing on the budget is currently slated for March 19th, though members flagged it may be too soon given other pending money articles.
Annual Town Meeting is set for May 2, 2026 at 9:00 a.m.
Next week's Finance Committee meeting will feature budget presentations from Schools and IT.

meetings.headline: FinCom previews FY27 budget: a level-service plan likely still needs an override, possibly again next year.
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee heard that the town's actual FY27 health insurance increase came in at 8.85% (down from over 20% after eliminating GLP-1 weight-loss drug coverage), and that a level-service town/school budget is unlikely to be balanced without an override. Members discussed how DPW, police, fire and school budgets will be presented in coming weeks, agreed to formally request the school department align its FY27 budget presentation with prior years and show FTEs and a consolidated athletics budget, and began a recurring discussion of how to structure a possible Proposition 2½ override, including the risk of needing another one next year. The committee also approved the January 8th minutes and adjourned by roll call vote.

budget_items.what_was_said: The actual health insurance rate increase came in at 8.85%, described as the actual (not estimated) figure just received.

Eliminating GLP-1 weight-loss drug coverage (voted by the insurance trust/'Maya') brought the increase down from an original estimate of over 20% to 8.85%; diabetes prescriptions for GLP-1s are still covered.

A committee member recalled that in a past budget year an extra $140,000 was paid toward transportation because it was being counted against the athletics revolving account, cited as a reason to want a consolidated athletics budget.
The chair explained that the level-service budget the committee will hear is likely not a balanced budget, and above-level-service or restorative requests will also be presented separately.

The chair described three possible budget scenarios the committee is dealing with: level service (likely requiring an override), increased/restorative service (a larger override), or a balanced budget reached through cuts.

The finance director said the level-service budget she is presenting already includes some cuts regardless of the override outcome, citing as an example a reduction from 5 days a week to 4 days a week of an unspecified service.
The chair opened discussion on a likely FY27 override or overrides, with no amount yet determined; a member argued level-service and restorative/enhanced requests should not be blended into one ask.
A member asked that the school present one consolidated athletics budget including expenses paid from the revolving account, a practice she said stopped around 2020.
The committee agreed to formally request that the FY27 school budget be presented in the same format as FY26 and FY25, clearly showing level service versus extra items and FTE per salary line.
A member raised concern that the Capital Planning Committee is reviewing a turf field replacement project that was never a ranked priority submitted by the school department, questioning the process.

The chair warned there is a high likelihood that even a level-service override passed this year could be followed by another level-service override next year, and floated setting the levy limit higher than taxed in year one to build headroom.

decisions.decision: DPW, police, and fire/facilities budgets are judged firm enough to present next week even though some union contracts (e.g., DPW Teamsters) are not yet finalized.

A committee member will draft and send the school business manager a written list of requests for how the FY27 school budget should be presented (aligned format with FY25/FY26, FTE per salary line, consolidated athletics budget, itemized approved budget changes).
The committee will consolidate all members' questions into one compiled list before sending them to the school business manager, rather than sending questions individually.

Because there will not be time to finish the full Finance Committee report before the warrant is mailed, the committee will include a high-level summary with a QR code in the mailed warrant and issue the full report about a month later.

meetings.headline: Monty Tech's FY27 assessment to Lunenburg would jump sharply, and the town manager warned an override is likely.
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee opened FY27 budget season by hearing Monty Tech's proposed budget, whose per-town assessment formula would raise Lunenburg's cost significantly more than Monty Tech's own budget grew; then heard a storm water task force pitch to create a dedicated storm water utility, which several committee members criticized as inefficient compared to funding it through the regular operating budget; and closed with a preliminary, free-cash-dependent FY27 capital plan and a town manager's report describing ongoing finance department turnover, an unclosed FY25 books, and a likely need for an override or cuts in FY27. No budget or override decisions were made; this was described as an early, non-binding discussion.

attendees.role: DPW director / storm water task force presenter

budget_items.topic: Monty Tech FY27 total proposed budget
budget_items.what_was_said: The business manager presented Monty Tech's total FY27 proposed budget as a 2.53% increase. She said most of the increase was driven by required net school spending and transportation costs.

budget_items.topic: Monty Tech total assessment to all 18 communities
budget_items.what_was_said: The total FY27 assessment to all member communities was presented, described as a 6% increase over FY26.

budget_items.topic: Lunenburg's FY27 assessment to Monty Tech
budget_items.what_was_said: Lunenburg's proposed FY27 assessment to Monty Tech was presented as an increase driven almost entirely by the state's required minimum contribution formula.
The business manager walked through the chapter 70 formula, noting Monty Tech's foundation aid calculation produced only a small increase, so the state applied a hold-harmless $75-per-pupil minimum.

budget_items.topic: Monty Tech capital budget cut to offset athletic complex lease
budget_items.what_was_said: The business manager said Monty Tech cut its capital budget to offset the new operating cost of the athletic field/track and bleacher tax-exempt municipal lease.

budget_items.topic: Monty Tech budget cuts from initial request
budget_items.what_was_said: The business manager said Monty Tech had to cut its initial wish-list budget request by this amount to reach the proposed FY27 budget.

budget_items.topic: Monty Tech excess and deficiency (E&D) use
budget_items.what_was_said: Monty Tech's certified E&D (similar to free cash) was presented, with portions proposed to offset the operating and capital assessments to towns.

budget_items.topic: Storm water utility proposed FY27 budget
budget_items.what_was_said: The DPW presenter proposed a storm water utility budget to reach MS4 compliance, versus continuing to fund storm water only through the existing DPW operating line.

budget_items.topic: Storm water project manager position cost
budget_items.what_was_said: A new storm water project manager position was costed out including salary, fringe benefits, and a share of the DPW director's salary and benefits.
Vendor costs for engineering, catch basin cleaning and roadway sweeping were presented as the largest share of the proposed storm water utility budget.
The task force proposed a flat annual fee for single-family homes, citing comparable towns' fees as a benchmark.
Twenty-two capital projects were submitted for FY27 across departments, ranked by the capital planning committee.
The town manager said the preliminary capital plan is funded using a conservative free cash estimate, level taxation, and the special purpose stabilization fund, pending free cash certification.

budget_items.topic: Free cash history used to estimate FY27 capital funding
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager cited 10-year and 5-year free cash averages and medians as the basis for a conservative FY27 free cash estimate.
The town manager described the special purpose stabilization fund, created in 2017 for vehicles/equipment, noting its current balance and that it has never been used.
The town manager reported the town is deficit-spending on snow and ice, already well over budget with much of winter remaining, which affects free cash available for other uses.
The town manager said TC Pacios building carries unbudgeted annual operating costs and that decommissioning half the building produced far less utility savings than expected.
The town manager flagged the FY27 mosquito control program assessment as a possible town meeting article given the town's financial condition.
The town manager reported a grant application for design funding for the Goodrich Street culvert.
The town manager reported a grant application for network infrastructure upgrades at the Adult Activity Center, a project unlikely to be funded within the FY27 capital plan itself.

decisions.decision: An additional capital planning committee meeting was scheduled for the following Wednesday to discuss initial reactions to the preliminary FY27 capital plan.

The chair asked department heads to include in their FY27 budget presentations: a summary of key services, a status-quo vs. proposed-changes summary, funding sources outside taxation, and an organizational chart.
A committee member agreed to collect finance committee members' detailed budget questions for each department and forward them to the town manager/finance director in advance of presentations.
The public schools budget presentation to the Finance Committee was set for February 19.
Warrant articles for the May 2 annual town meeting are due by March 16.
The town manager will begin meeting with TC Pacios building stakeholders (including cable access and the food pantry) starting the next day about winding down operations there.

meetings.headline: Superintendent warns prior budget cuts are pushing more students toward costly out-of-district special ed placements
meetings.summary: The committee heard a superintendent's report mixing a new DESE-funded reading tutoring grant with a warning that last year's cuts to in-district special education have left the district unable to serve some students, raising the risk of more out-of-district placements. The board discussed FY27 budget level-service figures, decided to stop applying for two small state family-engagement grants and hand them to a regional partner, voted to relocate meetings to the accessible middle-high school, gave the superintendent permission to explore redirecting a legislative earmark from passenger vans to ADA-accessible bathrooms at Turkey Hill, and heard principals describe strained staffing from prior cuts during school improvement plan updates.

meetings.headline: School officials call the FY25 surplus a budgeting failure, not lost money, and warn FY27 will be tight
meetings.summary: School committee members, the superintendent, the business manager and the town manager held a public forum to explain how the district ended FY25 with an unexpectedly large surplus, attributing it mainly to a competitive grant that freed up already-budgeted paraprofessional funds that were never reallocated, plus austerity measures imposed on a mistaken sense of scarcity. No formal votes were taken; officials described new oversight practices already adopted (regular budget updates, grant pre-approval, a new stabilization fund for out-of-district placements) and residents pressed on transparency, MCAS reading scores, and whether another override will be needed.

Out-of-district placement costs vary widely year to year and can shock the budget when a child moves into town after the budget closes.

The special stabilization account for out-of-district costs is established but currently unfunded; the operating budget line it backstops was estimated at this figure.

meetings.headline: Parks Commission voted to pay for an independent peer review of the skate park's roughly $1.14M cost estimate.
meetings.summary: The Parks Commission met to settle on a final project price for the privately-funded skate park so the nonprofit could proceed with bonding, reviewing an estimate of roughly $1.14 million from the skate park's consultant, Dillis and Roy. After extended discussion of risk, procurement law, and how a bond/security would actually function, the commission voted to authorize an independent peer review of the estimate (up to $6,000) and then heard a new skate park proposal to use a privately-backed cash escrow instead of a traditional bond, with details on renegotiating the lease agreement's security terms left to be worked out offline before returning to a public meeting.

meetings.headline: Town manager warns an FY27 override may be needed while unreconciled FY25 books risk losing state local aid
meetings.summary: The Select Board heard a lengthy town manager report warning that FY27 budget cost drivers exceed revenue growth and an override is likely, while the town's unsubmitted FY25 Schedule A risks the state withholding local aid and free cash remains uncertified. The board also honored a school resource officer for a cryptocurrency fraud recovery, marked a police officer's retirement, approved two peddler's licenses, voted to retain labor counsel under his new firm, and began discussing FY27 legislative earmark requests and warrant articles for town meeting.

budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager said health insurance, retirement assessment and school transportation are major cost drivers exceeding revenue growth, and that absent service reductions an override is likely required.
The town has not submitted the Schedule A to the Division of Local Services; failure to do so by February 13th risks the state withholding local aid.
Free cash has not yet been certified, which directly affects planning for town meeting including the capital plan, reserve transfers, and the snow and ice deficit.

A preliminary capital plan was delivered but is conservative pending free cash certification; two large projects, the Flatill road bridge and the public safety roof, are consuming much of the available funding.
The town is in deficit spending for snow and ice after 18 snow events this season; this is legally permitted deficit spending.
The DPW director and stormwater task force will present a proposed budget for a new storm water utility to the finance committee and later to a joint board meeting.
The town now bears full TCP building operating costs after the school department vacated; expected energy savings from partial decommissioning have not materialized.
The town applied for a MassDOT grant to fund design of the Goodrich Street culvert over Easterbrook Brook.
The town believes moving with Attorney Terry to his new, more public-sector-focused firm will be a cost savings over time; there are no hourly rates cited.
The board reviewed past state earmarks received by the town, mostly for schools, and discussed shifting focus toward town-side requests for the FY27 state budget.
A draft warrant article proposes a multi-year allocation for the town's 300th anniversary.
A second draft warrant article would establish a gift fund for donations and sale of anniversary merchandise.
The school committee discussed using funds originally for a new literacy coach position instead to build internal capacity by paying existing skilled staff stipends.
The school committee added a five-day preschool option alongside 2, 3, and 4-day options, with an annual tuition increase; this passed.
The school committee had discussed the school budget using certain healthcare figures, but has since learned those healthcare numbers are lower and will need to adjust the budget accordingly.

decisions.decision: Town manager to continue pursuing an official extension from DLS of the February 13th Schedule A deadline.
Town manager began meeting individually with TCP building user groups to discuss a possible wind-down of remaining building operations.
Chair will reach out to the school committee about crafting a joint warrant article on the Kids Kingdom relocation.
Deadline for other boards/committees to submit warrant articles for town meeting is set at March 16th.

It also opened discussion, without voting, on roughly doubling town beach fees to make the beach self-sustaining amid town budget pressure, and began reviewing draft field-use, signage, and non-resident field-fee policies to bring back at the next meeting.

what_happened.line: Town, school and finance officials agreed Lunenburg likely needs a property-tax override to close a projected FY27 gap, without settling on an amount or structure

why_it_matters: If the boards move forward, residents would eventually vote on an override, which raises the property tax bill outside the normal levy limit -- and the town's April 10th ballot deadline is setting the pace of these discussions.

The unresolved dispute over whether school staffing has grown or been cut touches what positions and services the school budget can protect, and residents will be asked to weigh that when an override figure is presented.

meetings.headline: Officials warn the FY27 budget leaves almost nothing after health insurance, pointing toward an override
meetings.summary: This was a joint Select Board / Finance Committee / School Committee ("tri-board") session in which the Town Manager walked through preliminary FY27 general government, debt, intergovernmental and revenue figures, including a new assistant town manager position, a large Munis/IT cost increase, and a steep audit-cost jump. The revenue walk-through showed that after health insurance is covered, almost no new money is left to fund any raises, cuts, or level services, and the group spent the second half of the meeting discussing operational efficiencies, the state and federal funding picture, and the likelihood that an override will be needed, without taking any substantive vote.

budget_items.what_was_said: The Town Manager said the select board budget is largely driven by staff covering the assistant town manager, HR/procurement director, executive assistant and minute clerks.

budget_items.topic: Select Board / Town Manager budget increase
budget_items.what_was_said: A modest select board increase was described as mostly expense-driven, while the town manager budget rises substantially due to the new assistant town manager position and a higher legal line.
The Town Manager proposed creating a standalone assistant town manager position, funded for half the year starting January 1, estimated near full-time cost if annualized.
A contracted services line created last year for staff appreciation is proposed to increase to give room for unforeseen contracted needs.
The FY26 accountant budget required a large special town meeting supplement due to transition costs, consultants and hiring, which the Town Manager said should not recur in FY27.
The finance department total was cited while discussing staffing changes including a retirement that offset new hires.
The audit line was said to have been underbudgeted; the actual FY27 audit cost is now expected to be much higher, partly because only two municipal auditors remain in Massachusetts.
Tax title is moving into the operating budget with no change in level funding; a request to restore treasurer/collector staff hours to 40 (from 36) drives a salary increase.

The FY26 IT budget was described as half a million dollars, and the preliminary FY27 IT budget increases further, driven mostly by Munis software costs and a reclassified communications/IT staff position.
The telephone budget line was raised to match actual cell phone and phone system bills, which had been historically underbudgeted.
A large increase to purchase of service is almost entirely Munis-driven; last year's upgrade cost was offset by ARPA which is not available this year, plus a contractual increase.
The on-site IT contractor line reflects five-days-a-week service; the Town Manager has already reduced to four days as of January and hopes to reduce further to three in FY27.
A line covers all townwide phone and cell phone bills across multiple carriers.
The FY27 budget is an election year and salary-driven, with an increase attributed mainly to election costs.
The finance committee's own budget was decreased slightly, while its training/reserve line was kept level from last year.
The salary reserve figure was called premature and not a real number, pending outcomes of active DPW, fire and clerical union negotiations and COLA decisions.

budget_items.topic: Town report / annual meeting booklet printing
budget_items.what_was_said: A large increase in the town report line was explained as covering both the report and the printing of annual/special town meeting booklets, not just the report itself.
Postage was consolidated into one line for the first time last year; it is currently running under budget and may be reduced if the trend holds.
The physicals budget for new hires, including heightened police/fire pre-employment screening, is being raised to align with actual year-to-date spending.
Total debt service is decreasing again in FY27 though by a smaller amount than the prior year's larger drop.
The Worcester County Regional retirement assessment is the main driver in intergovernmental costs and is a non-discretionary increase.

budget_items.topic: Land Use / building department permit revenue
budget_items.what_was_said: Building department fee revenue is projected roughly at recent average levels across permits, plumbing, electrical and gas.
Preliminary total FY27 revenue was presented, described as heavily reliant on property taxes.

budget_items.topic: Levy limit build-up (2.5%, new growth, excluded debt)
budget_items.what_was_said: The levy limit calculation adds the automatic Proposition 2½ increase, estimated new growth, and excluded debt on top before subtracting it back out on the expenditure side.
New growth for FY27 is estimated by the assessors, compared against last year's estimate versus higher actual new growth received.

State aid was presented at the current FY26 actual cherry sheet figure, covering Chapter 70, unrestricted government aid, library funding, school choice and veterans funding, held level pending the Governor's budget.
Local receipts (motor vehicle excise, meals tax, fees, fines, licensing) are being held level pending FY25 closeout, though investment income came in well above projection last year.
State assessments, school choice/library aid pass-throughs and the overlay reserve are subtracted off the top of revenue as non-appropriated, along with a pay-as-you-go capital contribution.

budget_items.topic: New revenue for FY27 and apportionment
budget_items.what_was_said: The remaining new revenue after FY26 appropriations was apportioned traditionally between school, town and Monty Tech by percentage share.

budget_items.topic: Health insurance impact on new revenue
budget_items.what_was_said: Subtracting projected non-discretionary health insurance increases for school and town from new revenue leaves only a small amount for all raises and new costs combined.
The town has been told to budget health insurance at a set percentage increase, which is what was used to reach the small remaining new-revenue figure.
A vehicle stabilization fund exists and part of the FY27 capital plan, including a needed ladder truck, is planned to draw from it.
A fire department budget request for an additional shift was described as not yet included in the presented numbers, at a stated additional cost.
Separate cost figures were cited for funding cost-of-living increases across the town's employee unions.
A finance committee member questioned why the town pays a large annual amount for recycling and suggested it as a possible operational efficiency.
The shared building referred to as TCP/TCPasios was said to cost more annually than the town currently has available in its operating budget.
The Town Manager's working figure for the outer bound of a potential override, before further cuts and efficiencies, was cited from the presentation.

meetings.headline: FinCom says FY27 leaves almost no room after health insurance; a school override looms and deep cuts are floated
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee heard that the finance/accounting office is in crisis (a departed finance director, an unclosed FY25, a retired accountant filling in part-time) and got an early FY27 revenue estimate that leaves very little after health insurance. Members debated whether to support another Proposition 2½ override, with one member insisting the town do "hard work" on cuts (recycling, the TCP building, ambulance receipts, capital funding sources) before any override is considered, while the town manager warned that a no-override budget likely means real staffing/service cuts. The committee also adjusted its budget-season calendar to bring Monty Tech and the schools in earlier, reviewed the capital plan ranking, water billing/enterprise fund problems, and approved its prior minutes and adjournment by roll call.

meetings.headline: Parks Commission tables the roughly $14 million Marshall Park project until town finances are clearer.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Parks Commission, meeting with only three of its members present, decided to replace the storm-damaged Fitzgerald Field sign and handed the long-stalled beach house dedication sign project to a newer member. Most of the meeting concerned deferring a decision on the large Marshall Park project until the town's overall financial picture is clearer, along with ongoing struggles to fill the vacant recreation director position and a plan to draft written field-use policies and forms, with no change to youth sports field fees this year.

A local company (Dillis) had agreed roughly two years ago to cover the cost of a new sign naming the beach house after Genevieve Nass; the chair said the project stalled and is handing it to Maryanne.

A board member said the town needs to understand its finances before pushing a project of that scale forward again at town meeting.

The vacant rec director position is a 19-hour-a-week job with no benefits; a member said covering the paperwork duties falls outside the volunteer commission's purview and suggested a stipend for whoever takes it on.

what_happened.line: The committee said it cannot sustain further staffing cuts and would not choose between a full-time athletic director/trainer and reading interventionists in the FY27 budget.
Members plan to vote their own FY27 school budget before the town manager sets her budget number, a change in sequencing from past years.
Any override request would go to the May town meeting rather than a November special town meeting, because November needs a higher approval threshold.
The committee voted to finalize its FY2025 budget variance statement, pending edits sent to the superintendent that do not change its message.
Officials disclosed a paraprofessional staffing gap in the current FY26 budget that had gone unaccounted for, but said the year should still close out okay.

why_it_matters: The choice between a full-time athletic director and reading interventionists is left open, so families may not know until later in the FY27 process which program gets funded.

An override, if requested, would appear on the May town meeting warrant rather than a November special vote, and this cycle's cuts would be discussed in broad categories rather than naming specific positions.
A paraprofessional undercount already found in the FY26 budget is a data gap worth watching for whether it recurs or grows in the FY27 numbers that underlie any override ask.

meetings.headline: Select Board rehired retired town accountant Karen Brochu as interim finance director amid a stalled recruitment.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board ratified Stephen Wallace as the new planning and economic development director, heard a clean FY24 audit from CBIZ that flagged behind-schedule cash and receivable reconciliations and an unresolved ~$90,000 Fitchburg water-billing issue, and approved bringing retired accountant Karen Brochu back part-time as interim finance director after the posted position drew no viable candidates. The board also approved several license renewals, an interim finance director's contract, and a letter to the Governor urging significantly more state local aid (citing a $351 million statewide UGGA ask) ahead of the FY2027 budget process, and opened discussion on the future redevelopment of 925 Mass Ave, appointment policy revisions, and opioid settlement fund planning.

attendees.role: director of planning and economic development (newly appointed), presenter

public_comment.topic: Asked whether the audit and Wallace introduction were public hearings, pressed for a public hearing on the $90,000 owed related to the Fitchburg water billing issue and on school department financial concerns, and criticized lack of interaction during public comment.
Asked what an 'intermittent heavy equipment operator' position is, and suggested the letter to the Governor should also press the state to fund unfunded state mandates.

Ratify the town manager's appointment of Brandy Oul as meal site manager.
Ratify the town manager's appointment of Joseph Davis as intermittent heavy equipment operator.
Approve the annual license renewals as printed on the agenda, with contingent votes for the applicants with outstanding items (excepting Smokestack, addressed separately).
Approve an additional annual common victualler license renewal that had been omitted from the agenda.
Approve the employment agreement for Karen Brochu as interim finance director/town accountant.
Approve the letter to Governor Healey on local aid and the FY2027 budget, and send copies to the Governor, legislators, the school committee and the finance committee.
Adjourn.

budget_items.what_was_said: The auditor reported the total general fund balance, with portions set aside for encumbrances and free cash used for the FY25 budget, leaving an unassigned balance that rose from the prior year.
The auditor listed balances in the general, zoning, vehicle and equipment, health insurance, and opioid stabilization funds, noting the general stabilization fund has grown steadily since 2013.
The auditor said real estate and personal property tax collections remained strong.
The auditor described a revenue surplus and underspending across departments, offset by use of free cash to balance the FY24 budget.
The town's OPEB trust contribution and investment income grew the fund, while the net OPEB liability fell, tied partly to a higher blended discount rate.

budget_items.topic: Net pension liability, Worcester Regional Retirement System
budget_items.what_was_said: The auditor reported the town's net pension liability rose slightly while the system's funded ratio improved.
Capital asset additions for general government, mainly road paving and equipment, were reported; none for the sewer enterprise.
Short-term debt outstanding funded the capital plan and a land purchase; required long-term debt payments for governmental and sewer funds were noted.
The town exceeded the federal expenditure threshold requiring a single audit, with the education stabilization fund selected for testing and no findings.
A resident and board members discussed money owed related to the town not raising water rates or billing timely when Fitchburg raised its rates; described as an FY25/26 issue outside the FY24 audit.
The town manager reported the MMA is calling for a statewide increase to UGGA to restore pre-recession local aid levels.

budget_items.topic: Finance director recruitment / recruiting agency fee
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager said Robert Half would be engaged to help recruit a finance director and payroll/benefits administrator, with a fee only if a hire results.
The board approved contingent votes for several license applicants with outstanding paperwork, inspections, or landlord issues.

budget_items.topic: Employment agreement, interim finance director Karen Brochu
budget_items.what_was_said: A retired former town accountant/finance director agreed to return on an hourly, part-time basis with no additional benefits, capped by retiree earnings limits.
A board member found the MMA's report basis for its ask, benchmarking UGGA against historical local tax share, yielding a similar but not identical figure to what was cited.
A board member reported a one-time reimbursement grant amount for Lunenburg from a fund tied to a regional hospital closure, based on a base amount plus a call-volume formula.
The planning board report noted a completed lot posted a performance guarantee bond, after which the certificate of occupancy could be issued.

decisions.decision: The town will engage CBIZ again for the FY25 audit once FY25 is closed, targeted for around January 31st, with a contract signed before work begins.
When engaging the auditor for FY25, the town manager will request special attention to issues including the Fitchburg water billing matter.
Board members indicated comfort proceeding with contingent votes on pending license renewals, including Lunenburg Gas, rather than delaying or calling a special meeting.
Board members will review the prior Mass Development presentation video (June 11) on 925 Mass Ave before the next discussion.
If any board member wants Mass Development's representative to give a follow-up presentation, they should tell the town manager before the following week.
The board's focus at the next 925 Mass Ave discussion will be the evaluation criteria on pages 16-17 of the draft RFP.
Board flagged for further consideration in January whether/how to structure a subcommittee to screen or interview appointment applicants, given open meeting law implications.
The appointment policy's key dates section will read simply 'June' rather than 'first and second Tuesday in June.'
A future agenda item will be scheduled to decide how the town will approach expenditure of opioid settlement funds.
Board members will coordinate signing the letter to the Governor via DocuSign or in person on another day, since it was not yet printed and a board member was absent.

what_happened.line: The board voted 4-1 to send the school and finance committees a letter pressing for better communication ahead of budget season, after friction at the recent special town meeting.
The board began rewriting its special events and appointment policies, including splitting event rules by size and loosening fixed deadlines for board appointments, without a final vote.
The board held off on remaining delinquent license renewals for one more week and may call a special meeting in late December if applicants have not come into compliance.
The board discussed but did not decide two unresolved items from the special town meeting: a water-billing rate increase for affected accounts and the Kids Kingdom playground redesign.
A resident used public comment to object that the board's stated reason for not reappointing a conservation commission member was not fact-checked.

why_it_matters: The tri-board letter could change how budget information reaches the school committee and finance committee before residents are asked to vote on next year's school budget.
A water-billing rate increase would land on the bills of the affected account holders, and the license-renewal delay affects local businesses awaiting town approval.
The Kids Kingdom redesign and the appointment-policy changes touch a town recreation project and the process by which residents get seated on town boards.

meetings.headline: Committee previews an FY27 school budget gap likely needing an override; also OK'd a costly France trip.
meetings.summary: The committee heard the superintendent's report (snow-day decisions, YTD spending, new Director of Teaching and Learning), then spent most of the meeting on money: a debated and approved France/Switzerland trip, a federal entitlement grants review flagging risk to Title I/II/IV and special-education grant funding, and a wide-ranging discussion of the FY27 budget, a likely override, and Turkey Hill's building future via the MSBA. Two routine policies (middle school pathway exploration; competency determination) passed on third read, and Turkey Hill accessibility needs were flagged as needing near-term attention regardless of the MSBA timeline.

meetings.headline: Select Board voted unanimously to let the town manager sign a low-income community solar discount deal.
meetings.summary: The Select Board heard a presentation from the new LEAF education nonprofit and voted unanimously to authorize the town manager to sign onto a Colonial Power Group low-income solar (SMART) discount program. The board also reviewed a draft tri-board communication letter ahead of a budget season expected to be difficult, discussed the finance department's ongoing staffing transition, license renewals, and heard committee reports including the school committee's plan to build three FY27 budget scenarios, before voting to enter executive session on firefighter union bargaining.

budget_items.what_was_said: LEAF, a new citizen-led nonprofit, described its mission to raise private/corporate money for direct grants to teachers outside the district's regular budget. No specific fundraising totals were given.

Colonial Power described a state SMART program giving UNITIL's already-qualified low-income customers an extra discount on top of the existing municipal aggregation rate, illustrated with hypothetical figures.

The school committee increased the substitute teacher daily rate to try to attract more substitutes.

budget_items.topic: Capital plan / primary school feasibility studies
budget_items.what_was_said: The Capital Planning Committee approved its capital plan and heard about primary school entry/driveway and playground equipment feasibility studies.
The district will produce three FY27 budget scenarios: a level service budget, a level funded budget, and a prioritized necessary increase budget.
The school committee discussed health insurance cost projections potentially rising significantly for the coming year.
A stretch of local road was noted as newly eligible for National Highway Freight Network funding, which could in theory fund improvements to a treacherous intersection.

meetings.headline: Select Board voted a single FY2026 tax rate, rejecting a split rate and all optional exemptions.
meetings.summary: The Select Board held its annual FY2026 tax classification public hearing, at which the principal assessor recommended and the board voted a single tax rate with no residential exemption, open space discount, or small commercial exemption. Public comment also raised concerns about the poorly-run finance committee warrant hearing and about unaccounted Fitchburg charges going undetected for years, urging tighter accounting oversight ahead of budget season.

Argued for a split tax rate, citing the tax deferral program for seniors and the need for revenue to fund services such as the senior center.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to set a single FY2026 tax rate for all property classes, rejecting a split rate and all optional exemptions.
Board members signaled they would follow the assessor's recommendation before the formal vote was taken.
The board first closed the tax classification public hearing by unanimous vote after the assessor walked through valuations and the levy calculation.

why_it_matters: A single tax rate means residential and commercial property owners share the same rate rather than shifting more of the levy onto commercial parcels, which shapes what every FY2026 tax bill looks like.
Declining the residential exemption, open space discount, and small commercial exemption means no separate tax break exists this year for owner-occupants, open land, or small qualifying businesses.
The accounting concerns raised about the finance committee hearing and Fitchburg charges point to oversight questions the board may face again as budget season begins.

meetings.headline: District previews FY27-29 outlook, asking to restore staff cut in FY26; no vote was taken.
meetings.summary: The select board, finance committee and school committee met jointly to hear a preliminary, forward-looking FY27-29 school budget outlook, explicitly deferring any FY25 questions to a later public forum. The superintendent and business manager walked through contractual assumptions (salaries, health insurance, utilities, transportation) and a series of requested staff restorations -- interventionists, a kindergarten paraprofessional, a world-language teacher, a music teacher, a bridge/TLC program, an ELL teacher, and a debated full-time athletic director/assistant principal split -- framed as restoring FY26 cuts rather than new expansion. No formal votes were taken on any budget item; the boards adjourned after discussion, with several follow-up items assigned to the administration for the next budget cycle.

minutes.headline: Town meeting reversed a failed vote to pay Fitchburg the water bills Lunenburg forgot to send for over a year
minutes.summary: This special town meeting worked through 17+ warrant articles, most contentiously a near-failed then reconsidered vote to pay Fitchburg for water bills the town had failed to send to 11 accounts for over a year, plus a $195,790.97 FY26 budget amendment driven by heavy finance-department staff turnover. what_happened.line: Town meeting rejected, then reconsidered and passed, paying Fitchburg for water bills the town failed to send to 11 accounts for over a year.
Town meeting approved a mid-year FY26 budget amendment driven by turnover of the finance director, assistant accountant, and payroll coordinator.
Town meeting created a special education out-of-district reserve fund over the finance committee's own recommendation against it.

The new special education reserve fund is a standing account town meeting still controls dollar by dollar, meant to absorb the swings in out-of-district placement costs that have come up in three straight budget seasons.
The MBTA Communities zoning overlay is a compliance vote, not a building proposal by itself, but it sets the multifamily density allowed at Tritown going forward.

Discussion of Article 3 (payment of prior year bills) uncovered a long-standing failure to properly bill City of Fitchburg water customers, resulting in a large accrued bill with interest; the board deferred a recommendation on that article until its meeting the next day, ahead of special town meeting.

meetings.headline: Finance Committee splits on scrapping the Personnel Committee; defers most Nov. 18 warrant articles to Town Meeting
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee held its public hearing on the warrant for the November 18 special town meeting, going article by article. It approved several routine transfers, deferred a number of contested or under-documented articles (a stormwater consulting appropriation, a special education reserve fund, a senior tax deferral expansion, and two salary-plan articles) so the town manager could present more detail at Town Meeting, and split its votes on a proposal to change how warrants are distributed and on a proposal to eliminate the Personnel Committee.

Its vote on eliminating the volunteer Personnel Committee and shifting its authority to the town manager ended inconclusive, roughly one in favor, two opposed, one deferring.
The committee voted, 3-2, not to recommend replacing mailed warrant booklets with a postcard notice, a change pitched as a mailing-cost saving.
It approved, 3-1, a transfer to hire outside consultants for capital project cost estimating, after debate over how the funding moves between capital accounts.

why_it_matters: Residents at the Nov. 18 special town meeting will vote on the deferred articles -- special education reserve funding, senior tax deferral eligibility, and salary-plan changes -- without a Finance Committee recommendation attached.
Eliminating the Personnel Committee would move authority over town personnel and salary administration to the town manager, a governance change separate from any single budget line.
How town meeting warrants get distributed -- full booklet or mailed notice -- affects how residents learn what they're being asked to vote on.

meetings.headline: Committee begins staged process to decide whether to renovate or replace Turkey Hill Elementary, no vote yet
meetings.summary: This School Committee meeting covered routine business (transfers, donations, minutes) and the superintendent's report before moving into an extended discussion of long-term facilities planning. The bulk of the meeting was a debate over how to decide the future of Turkey Hill Elementary (renovate vs. rebuild) and how MSBA reimbursement works, ending with an agreed staged process rather than a decision; the committee also took first readings of four policies and heard a Trust Fund Commission chairman ask that all school-related gift/trust records be turned over for review.

meetings.headline: Town manager says finance-department transition is causing substantial, monthslong operational and financial disruption
meetings.summary: The Select Board heard a Lunenburg Snow Riders equipment gift, ratified three town-hire appointments, and voted to sign a Massachusetts Teachers Association-linked advocacy letter to the state legislature on FY27 school funding over one member's objection about scope and a resident's objection about partisanship. The board worked through special-town-meeting warrant articles (voting recommendations on two planning board articles), heard the town manager describe a difficult and costly finance-department staffing transition and a corrected new-growth figure, and set up scheduling for a pre-town-meeting session and a tri-board meeting with the schools before entering executive session on a non-union personnel matter.

A reader should also check the sick-leave language change, since the official minutes note the terms were "harmonized" without saying which term ("doctor's note" vs. "doctor's certificate") was kept, and whether the three-consecutive-day threshold was actually changed or just discussed.

findings.official: A transition mechanism was introduced whereby unused vacation time as of July 1, 2026, would be converted into a one-time vacation bank, with employees required to use at least one-third of that bank during each of fiscal years 2027, 2028, and 2029. Employees carrying balances over 120 hours as of June 30, 2026, would receive a lump-sum buyout of all time in excess of 120 hours.
findings.note: A substantive policy decision entirely absent from our minutes; worth confirming it was accurately captured for anyone relying on our record of Article 16.

findings.about: Personnel Committee quorum authority shifting to Select Board (SAP Section 70-12)
findings.official: Language was added providing that, in the event the Personnel Committee lacks sufficient members to conduct business, the Select Board shall have authority to administer the relevant provision of the SAP.
findings.note: Not captured in our minutes at all; a governance change worth noting for Article 16/17 context given the personnel committee is also the subject of Article 17.

findings.about: holiday pay clarifying language retained after discussion (SAP Section E)

what_happened.line: The board voted to recommend Article 16, rewriting Salary Administration Plan rules on vacation banking, sick leave, grievances and job descriptions.
Article 17, consolidating personnel-committee authority, passed 4-1 to recommend after review of labor counsel's changes.
The town manager told the finance committee the new vacation-bank language carries a financial impact still being calculated.
Article 4, funding storm water consulting from an unexpended capital project, was voted in, reconsidered, then re-voted after an objection.
Article 5, a cable committee fund transfer plus added videographer funding, passed unanimously to include and recommend.

why_it_matters: Articles 16 and 17 rewrite town personnel policy on vacation, sick leave and grievances -- residents vote on them at the Nov. 18 special town meeting.
The vacation-bank change carries a cost to the town that was not yet quantified when the finance committee took it up.
The storm water consulting article is a step toward a possible stormwater utility fee, a mechanism that could show up on future bills.

meetings.headline: Finance Committee reviewed all 17 special town meeting warrant articles, deferring recommendations to the Nov. 13 public hearing
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Finance Committee walked through all 17 articles of the special town meeting warrant (FY26 budget amendments, transfers, a special education reserve fund, a 41A tax deferral expansion, MBTA zoning compliance, and several SAP/personnel bylaw changes), asking questions but deliberately deferring any recommendations until the November 13th public hearing. The only formal votes taken were procedural: approving three sets of prior tri-board minutes and adjournment.

budget_items.what_was_said: Outside CPA firm Eric Kincherf CPA will complete the entire FY25 closeout; free cash likely will not be certified by special town meeting, but no free-cash appropriations are planned so there should be no impact.

Governor Healey's reported pullback of local earmarks did not affect Lunenburg's two earmarks, which have now flowed to the state agencies; the town requested the funds quickly in case they are pulled back.

budget_items.what_was_said: Transfers from salary reserve are planned for the police chief, the new finance director, and police wages from collective bargaining.

budget_items.what_was_said: New growth actuals are coming in well above the budgeted estimate, prompting a raise-and-appropriate; members disputed the exact figure.

A bill from Heywood Hospital for employee health needs a 9/10 vote at special town meeting; recommended deferral to town meeting.
Additional funds are needed for stormwater/MS4 consulting after switching consultants, to be transferred from unexpended prior-year capital (ADA Ritter project).
A pass-through of retained earnings to the general fund and back for PAC-related expenses is being cleaned up into a direct transfer from retained earnings to the enterprise fund.
An additional new amount is being added for PAC's videographer staffing on top of the retained-earnings transfer.
PAC's fee revenue is running well below its budget/retained-earnings draw, raising concern about sustaining operations on declining cable receipts.
Funds from the cemetery sale-of-lots account will be transferred to the capital article fund to straighten and repair headstones.
A standalone fund is proposed to hire professional project estimators for capital projects, after several in-house estimates came in far under actual bids.

budget_items.what_was_said: The proposed reserve fund cannot exceed a stated share of annual net school spending; article establishes but does not fund the reserve.

budget_items.what_was_said: A prior town meeting lowered the deferral interest rate; this article proposes raising the income eligibility threshold to match 100% of the state circuit-breaker amount.
Printing and mailing the full warrant booklet to all households costs an estimated amount annually, cited as a reason to switch to a postcard notice.

budget_items.topic: Article 16 - SAP vacation system transition cost
budget_items.what_was_said: Changing employees over to a new vacation accrual system under the redrafted personnel bylaw will carry a cost that has not yet been quantified pending the attorney's final draft.

New growth for FY26, originally projected at $400,000, appears to be coming in around $1.3 million, driven by corrected assessed values and personal property findings; not yet confirmed with the assessor.

meetings.headline: Parks Commission held off deciding the skate park bond amount, deferring to Chris Ruth's review first
meetings.summary: The Parks Commission discussed repeated vandalism and a proposed noise-deterrent device at Wallace Park, then spent most of the meeting on the Marshall Park skate park project: whether to require a costly completion bond or a much cheaper restorative bond, and concerns that the master plan's new park location will change once construction begins. what_happened.line: Select Board voted 3-2 to pull the APDC/Historical Commission merger article from the special town meeting warrant.
The vote followed extended public opposition and a town counsel review of legal questions the merger raised.
The board voted 4-1 to recommend the special education reserve fund article, after a member flagged a possible hidden future budget impact.
The noise ordinance article was deferred and will not appear on this warrant, pending further work.
The board voted to include and recommend the 41A senior tax deferral article, raising the decades-old income threshold for that exemption.

why_it_matters: Pulling the merger article means the Architectural Preservation District Commission keeps separate authority over historic-district reviews, at least until a future town meeting takes it up again.
The 41A article, if approved by voters at the November 18 special town meeting, would let more senior homeowners qualify to defer their property tax bills.
The special education reserve fund article changes how the town could set aside money for special-ed costs; it carries no budget impact yet, but a member noted it could down the road.

meetings.headline: Committee reversed itself, voting to let soccer teams wear the new uniforms already purchased
meetings.summary: The School Committee accepted PTO donations, a state legislative earmark for primary-school touch screens and restoring I-Ready, and reversed a prior vote to release new soccer uniforms to players this season. The bulk of the meeting covered an assessment/accountability report showing concerning third-grade reading and special-education scores linked partly to prior budget cuts, followed by the superintendent's FY28 budget priorities, her first-year evaluation goals, and a discussion setting draft committee goals around Turkey Hill's future, capital planning, and a more reasoned budget-decision process.

budget_items.what_was_said: The parent-teacher organization donated funds to each school, left to each principal's discretion, and the committee voted to accept three such donations.
The superintendent described a one-time, non-recurring earmark from state legislators that cannot be added to the base budget; the captions gave inconsistent figures for the total and its two pieces.
The superintendent proposed spending part of the earmark on touch screens for every primary school classroom, the only school without them, replacing projectors.
The superintendent proposed restoring I-Ready diagnostic and instructional access for at least one more year; asked the cost, she said it was about 47.

The district considered using the earmark for smaller transportation vans instead, but determined the cost would exceed the available money and require driver stipends and special licenses, so it was not pursued.
Members noted the athletic fee was previously increased and is intended to partially cover uniform costs, though it does not cover the full cost.

The district previously cut a single dedicated Wilson reading position at Turkey Hill and instead used training funds to certify multiple inclusion teachers district-wide in the Wilson reading system.

Members discussed that compensation, especially for paraprofessionals, is weak compared to other districts, making positions hard to fill, though the superintendent cited staff loyalty to Lunenburg as a mitigating factor.

budget_items.topic: Teacher and instructional staff retention rate
budget_items.what_was_said: The superintendent set a goal of 90% or higher staff retention; last year's rate, which included layoffs, was described as concerningly low.
A member asked about anticipated multi-year budget impacts as union contracts, capped at three-year terms, come up for renewal; the business manager is building this into the long-term forecast.
The superintendent said she is conservatively forecasting entitlement grant funding to come in lower next year given uncertainty at the federal level.

budget_items.topic: Turkey Hill Elementary renovation cost estimate
budget_items.what_was_said: A member cited a prior renovation estimate for Turkey Hill, calling it likely too low, while pushing the committee to commit to a renovate-or-rebuild direction.
A warrant article is expected proposing the school committee give up budget responsibility for Kids Kingdom; a member said this would make the school budget more realistic.

The superintendent's first-year evaluation goals will be a formal action item at next month's meeting.

Rather than a strict numeric formula, the committee leaned toward a small set of guiding questions/rubric, building on the superintendent's five budget-priority questions, to weigh competing budget requests.
A member will draft written testimony on the statewide K-2 (Chapter 70) school finance formula for the committee to review, to potentially submit to the state working group.
The committee will talk with the facilities director about Turkey Hill as a next step.

meetings.summary: The Select Board worked through the warrant for the November 18 special town meeting, deferring several articles (special education reserve fund, a proposed APDC/historical commission merger, and a new noise ordinance) pending more input from the finance committee, town counsel, and affected committees. It also split a large salary-plan overhaul into two articles to separate the elimination of the personnel committee from employee-benefit fixes, approved routine licenses and warrants, and heard public comment on government transparency, a protest event, and remembrances of two centenarians before entering executive session on a litigation matter.

public_comment.topic: Invited people to a second No Kings Day protest and criticized federal government actions.

public_comment.stated_role: chair of the planning board, speaking as a citizen
public_comment.topic: Urged caution on the proposed warrant article merging the APDC with the Historical Commission.
Praised the town manager's collaborative approach and highlighted work of the Council on Aging and senior center staff.
Marked the deaths of two town centenarians and thanked the library for its 20th anniversary events.
Urged the board to give warrant articles (APDC merger, noise ordinance, personnel committee elimination) more public vetting before town meeting.

Include Article H (project estimator appropriation) in the warrant.
Defer Article I (special education reserve fund).
Approve the minutes of September 23, 2025.
Enter executive session under MGL c.30 s.21A(3) to discuss litigation strategy (Department of Industrial Accidents claim) and not return to open session.

The town manager confirmed a cost overage on the school mini-split project, to be combined with the storm water article into one funding-flexible warrant article.

The town manager said each use of a project estimator costs roughly this much and proposed a lump sum to cover several years of DPW, school and town facilities estimates.
The board discussed raising income ceilings for the senior property tax deferral program to match circuit breaker maximums and reaffirmed a previously voted lower interest rate.
The town manager explained a prior RFP for the assessing project drew no bidders and proposed creating a temporary employee position instead, using funds already appropriated at May town meeting.

what_happened.line: The board set a special meeting for November 17 to vote on several deferred warrant articles ahead of the November 18 special town meeting.
A vote on merging the APDC with the Historical Commission was put off, with full membership of both bodies invited to next week's discussion.
A proposed noise ordinance was also held over, pending a town counsel redraft and possible input from the police chief.

A broader salary administration plan overhaul was split into two articles, separating elimination of the personnel committee from other salary and benefit changes.

why_it_matters: Several warrant articles going to the November 18 special town meeting are not yet finalized, including proposals affecting town committee structure and noise rules.
Splitting the salary plan article means the personnel committee's elimination will be voted on separately from other employee-benefit changes.
Residents who want input on the APDC/historical commission merger or the noise ordinance have another chance before the November 17 special board meeting.

meetings.headline: Finance Committee pushed back on rushing Personnel Committee/APDC bylaw changes to November Town Meeting
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee spent most of the meeting reviewing two Special Town Meeting warrant articles proposed by the Town Manager -- eliminating the Personnel Committee and merging the APDC into the Historical Commission -- with a member arguing both need more public process before going to voters, and the committee agreeing to vote on the full warrant at its next meeting (Oct. 23) ahead of the Nov. 18 Special Town Meeting. Members also discussed FY26 school budget growth compared to FY25 actuals, long-term facilities/capital planning (Turkey Hill, Ritter/Town Hall building costs), separation of the town accountant and finance director roles, and approved prior tri-board meeting minutes.

budget_items.topic: Special Town Meeting warrant: eliminate Personnel Committee
budget_items.what_was_said: A member argued eliminating the Personnel Committee is too big a change to make without more public input and comparison to other towns' experience.

budget_items.topic: Special Town Meeting warrant: merge APDC into Historical Commission
budget_items.what_was_said: A member raised concerns about folding the Architectural/Preservation Design Commission's function into the Historical Commission without a public process.

budget_items.topic: FY26 school budget vs FY25 actuals
budget_items.what_was_said: A member said the schools' FY26 budget is well above FY25 actual spending, calling it a large one-year increase on a roughly $25 million budget.

budget_items.topic: FY25 override plus increase, two-year total
budget_items.what_was_said: The same member noted FY25 included the override plus an additional increase, adding up to a large combined increase over two years.

budget_items.topic: Ritter/Town Hall building cost estimating approach
budget_items.what_was_said: A member suggested using a rough-order-of-magnitude cost-per-square-foot estimate rather than paying for full architectural design work upfront.
Members worried that redesign costs on town building projects have been paid multiple times over and cautioned against spending heavily on plans that go unused.
A member recalled the earlier building project estimate was set deliberately high so the town would not later be asked for significantly more money.

budget_items.topic: Possible solar panel revenue on parking lot
budget_items.what_was_said: If extra money were available from the building project, the committee had discussed adding solar panels on a parking lot to generate revenue.

budget_items.topic: Special Town Meeting hearing timing requirement
budget_items.what_was_said: Members discussed whether a finance committee hearing on money articles must be posted a set number of days before the Special Town Meeting.

decisions.decision: Committee agreed it does not need to vote on the Special Town Meeting warrant articles at this meeting; a vote will happen at a later meeting before the November Town Meeting.
Several members agreed the Personnel Committee and APDC warrant articles are premature for the November Special Town Meeting and should wait, possibly until the May Annual Town Meeting.
Committee agreed to ask the tri-board presenters to send budget presentation materials about a week ahead of the meeting rather than the day of.

Committee decided not to align itself with other committees' individual bylaws/policies when responding to the master plan steering committee questionnaire, since Finance only reviews financial impact.
Committee determined the next meeting, October 23rd, will serve as the vote/hearing on the Special Town Meeting warrant, to meet the 14-day requirement before the November 18th Town Meeting.
